questions.question: What distinguishes an FPTAS from a PTAS?
options: An FPTAS is polynomial in input size and 1/ε
A PTAS may return infeasible solutions
A PTAS cannot use dynamic programming
questions.why: An FPTAS requires joint polynomial dependence on |I| and 1/ε.
questions.readingLabel: Related W–S §3.1 lecture: the FPTAS running-time requirement

teaching.summary: Both schemes preserve feasibility and approach the optimum as ε decreases. A PTAS permits an input-size exponent depending on 1/ε; an FPTAS requires a polynomial jointly in the input bit length and 1/ε. For example, n^(1/ε) is polynomial for every fixed ε but fails the joint requirement.
steps: Separate the quality guarantee from the running-time guarantee.
Compare n^(1/ε) with n³/ε as functions of both parameters.
Check arithmetic bit lengths as well as the number of DP states.
distractors: An FPTAS approximates within the specified error and need not return OPT.
Correct: joint polynomial dependence distinguishes fully polynomial schemes.
Both PTAS and FPTAS guarantees require a feasible output.
Dynamic programming is allowed; its state range and bit complexity determine whether the scheme is fully polynomial.
teaching.takeaway: A fixed-accuracy polynomial algorithm need not remain polynomial when accuracy is part of the input.
teaching.followup: Explain why the exact capacity-indexed knapsack DP is pseudo-polynomial.

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: For a minimization LP relaxation, the LP optimum is…
questions.why: Relaxing integrality enlarges the feasible region; the minimum cannot increase.
questions.readingLabel: Related lecture: minimization and maximization relaxation conventions

teaching.summary: Relaxation enlarges the feasible region. For minimization, the old feasible solutions remain available and new ones may improve the objective downward, so the LP optimum is a lower bound on integral OPT. This bound is useful only when paired with a feasible rounded solution and a proved upper comparison to its LP value.
steps: Embed every integral feasible solution in the relaxed feasible set.
Use that minimization over a superset cannot give a larger minimum.
Keep the reverse upper-bound convention for maximization separate.
distractors: This is the wrong direction for a minimization relaxation.
Correct: LP≤OPT because the relaxed feasible set contains the integral one.
Equality requires integrality or an instance-specific argument and is not automatic.
The feasible-set inclusion provides a definite objective comparison.
teaching.takeaway: The direction of an LP bound is determined by the objective direction and feasible-set inclusion.
teaching.followup: For MAX-CUT, is the SDP optimum a lower or an upper bound on integral OPT?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: Which inequality uses the least-loaded-machine choice?
questions.why: At job j’s placement, every machine load was at least S, hence the earlier total load was at least mS.
questions.readingLabel: Related W–S §3.2: load lower bounds; list scheduling is additional background

teaching.summary: If job j starts on a least-loaded machine at load S, every machine’s current load is at least S. The work already assigned is thus at least mS. Bounding that work by all jobs except j gives the displayed inequality; it is the step that actually uses the algorithm’s machine choice.
steps: Fix the job whose completion is being analyzed and its start load S.
Use the least-loaded choice to lower-bound every current machine load by S.
Sum those m loads and compare with total work excluding j.
distractors: The job-size lower bound on OPT is true independently of the machine-selection rule.
Correct: least-loaded choice makes mS no larger than previously assigned work.
Every feasible schedule has cost at least OPT; this does not use least-loaded placement.
This loose expression is not the crucial load inequality used in the proof.
teaching.takeaway: Identify the precise line where an algorithmic choice enters the analysis.
teaching.followup: Derive S≤(total work−pⱼ)/m from the chosen answer.

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: For m=3, the list-scheduling bound is…
questions.readingLabel: Related W–S §3.2: averaging and the final-job overshoot

teaching.summary: The standard list-scheduling ratio is 2−1/m, giving 5/3 for three machines. It comes from C=S+pⱼ≤total/m+(1−1/m)pⱼ, followed by two distinct lower bounds on OPT: total work divided by m and the largest job. This is a list-scheduling guarantee, not the accuracy-parameter guarantee of the assigned PTAS.
steps: Use least-loaded placement to bound the last job’s start.
Separate the average-load term from the coefficient of its processing time.
Substitute m=3 into 2−1/m.
distractors: Three halves is the m=2 standard bound, not the m=3 expression.
Four thirds is stronger than this general list-scheduling theorem provides.
Two is a valid weaker bound, but it discards the refinement 1/m requested by the standard formula.
teaching.takeaway: Two different OPT lower bounds can combine into one approximation factor.
teaching.followup: Why does the coefficient of pⱼ become 1−1/m rather than one?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: For jobs [8,7,6,5,4], what is the average-load lower bound with m=3?
questions.why: Total work is 30, divided by 3 gives 10.
questions.readingLabel: Related W–S §3.2: the original-volume lower bound

teaching.summary: The five processing times sum to 30. Any schedule on three machines has a maximum load at least its average load, 30/3=10. The bound is independent of how an algorithm orders jobs; it need not be attainable because indivisible jobs may prevent a perfectly balanced partition.
steps: Add all processing requirements before considering assignments.
Divide by the number of machines.
Use maximum load≥average load for every feasible schedule.
distractors: Eight is the maximum-job lower bound, a different quantity.
Nine is below the actual average load ten.
Correct: total work thirty divided by three is ten.
Twelve may arise in particular assignments but is not the volume average.
teaching.takeaway: A lower bound can be valid without describing a realizable schedule.
teaching.followup: Can you partition these five jobs into three machine loads all at most ten?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: Items have total size 11.2 in unit-capacity bins. Which is the strongest immediate integer lower bound from volume alone?
questions.readingLabel: W–S §3.3: volume and additive-bin accounting

teaching.summary: Each unit-capacity bin holds total size at most one. Packing volume 11.2 therefore needs at least 11.2 bins in the fractional counting inequality, and integrality strengthens this to twelve. This lower bound is not an exact optimum formula: the arrangement of indivisible item sizes may require more bins.
steps: Write B≥11.2 from total capacity B.
Use B integer to round the lower bound upward.
Avoid turning a necessary condition into a constructive upper bound.
distractors: OPT≥11 is true but weaker; the strongest immediate integer volume bound is twelve.
Correct: ceiling the total volume gives twelve.
Capacity volume provides a lower bound, not an upper bound.
Equality would need a feasible twelve-bin packing and is not implied by volume alone.
teaching.takeaway: Ceilings strengthen integral lower bounds, but do not prove attainability.
teaching.followup: Construct item sizes with integer total volume whose optimum needs strictly more bins than that total.

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: ALG≤1.1OPT+5 is…
questions.why: An additive constant is allowed in an asymptotic performance guarantee.
questions.readingLabel: W–S §3.3: absolute versus asymptotic guarantees

teaching.summary: The additive five bins prevent claiming an absolute ratio of 1.1 on every input. Dividing by OPT gives ALG/OPT≤1.1+5/OPT, whose excess term tends to zero as the optimum grows. This says nothing by itself about fully polynomial running time or a family of arbitrary accuracies.
steps: Retain the additive term when writing the finite-instance guarantee.
Divide the entire inequality by OPT.
Interpret the limit for large OPT, rather than suppressing the term on small instances.
distractors: An absolute ratio would require ALG≤1.1OPT with no additive loss.
Correct: the additive constant belongs to an asymptotic guarantee.
An FPTAS includes an accuracy family and a joint polynomial-time condition not stated here.
The inequality bounds an algorithmic solution; it is not an infeasibility witness.
teaching.takeaway: The exact form of the guarantee matters more than its leading constant alone.
teaching.followup: For OPT=10, what ratio bound does this inequality actually give?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: Which defining metric-TSP property is used by the general shortcutting proof?
questions.why: Triangle inequality prevents the shortcut from increasing length.
questions.readingLabel: Additional background: metric-TSP shortcutting; not assigned planar MIS §10.2

teaching.summary: The general metric-TSP proof replaces a multi-edge walk segment by the direct edge between its endpoints. Repeated triangle inequality makes the direct distance no greater than the segment length. Unit edge lengths are a special sufficient case because they also satisfy triangle inequality; the general defining metric property is the intended answer.
steps: Name the two endpoints and the path segment being replaced.
Apply triangle inequality repeatedly along that segment.
Use nonincrease of each replacement to shortcut the whole walk.
distractors: Bipartiteness does not bound a direct edge by the length of an alternative path.
Correct: triangle inequality supplies the needed endpoint-distance comparison.
Unit lengths also satisfy triangle inequality, but are a special case rather than the general defining metric property.
Planarity alone does not control edge lengths along alternative paths.
teaching.takeaway: State the structural hypothesis at the exact transformation it supports.
teaching.followup: Give three edge lengths violating triangle inequality for which a direct shortcut increases cost.

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: Why is the minimum matching on odd-degree MST vertices at most OPT/2?
options: Optimal tour splits into two O-joins, one ≤ OPT/2
questions.why: The optimal tour can be partitioned into two O-joins; their lengths sum to OPT. In a metric closure, the min perfect matching is no worse than an O-join.
questions.readingLabel: Additional background: Christofides and metric matching; outside the current assigned sections

teaching.summary: The odd-degree MST vertex set has even cardinality. Visit those vertices in their optimal-tour order and shortcut between consecutive ones using the metric inequality. Alternating edges of this even cycle form two perfect matchings whose combined cost is at most OPT, so one costs at most OPT/2; the minimum matching is no more expensive.
steps: Restrict the optimal tour to the even odd-degree vertex set, using metric shortcutting.
Split the resulting even cycle into its two alternating matchings.
Choose the cheaper matching and compare with the minimum matching.
distractors: Odd degree identifies vertices requiring parity repair; it does not make edges free.
Correct: the alternating O-join or matching comparison splits a total cost at most OPT into two pieces.
The MST need not cost half of OPT; only MST≤OPT follows generally.
Some matchings can be expensive; the bound comes from constructing two comparison matchings.
teaching.takeaway: An existence comparison to a cheaply chosen witness bounds the optimum of a subproblem.
teaching.followup: Where does the even cardinality of the odd-degree set enter this argument?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: What fraction of 3-literal clauses is satisfied in expectation by a uniform random assignment (distinct noncomplementary literals)?
questions.why: Only one of the 2³ truth patterns falsifies all three literals.
questions.readingLabel: W–S §§5.1–5.3: random-clause calculation

teaching.summary: A three-literal clause on distinct variables fails only when all three literals are false, an event of probability 1/8. Its satisfaction indicator therefore has expectation 7/8. The assumption about distinct noncomplementary literals prevents confusing repeated variables or tautologies with three independent failure events.
steps: Translate clause failure into simultaneous literal falsity.
Multiply three independent probabilities one half.
Subtract failure from one to obtain the expected indicator value.
distractors: One half is the one-literal success probability.
Three quarters is the distinct two-literal success probability.
Correct: one minus one eighth is seven eighths.
Certainty would require a tautology or another stronger property not assumed here.
teaching.takeaway: Check clause simplification before using 1−2^−k.
teaching.followup: How can you compute the expected weighted number of satisfied clauses even when their indicators are dependent?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: What enables a deterministic choice preserving conditional expectation?
options: The two conditional expectations average to the current one
questions.why: Conditioning on the next unbiased bit partitions the current expectation into two equally weighted conditional expectations.
questions.readingLabel: W–S §§5.1–5.3: conditional-expectation invariant

teaching.summary: The current expected objective is a weighted average of its two conditional values after exposing the next bit. For an unbiased bit the weights are one half each, so at least one conditional value is no smaller than the current expectation. Choosing it deterministically preserves the invariant; computing the conditional values efficiently remains an algorithmic requirement.
steps: Condition on the partial assignment already fixed.
Partition by the next bit and apply the tower property.
Select a branch at least as large as the average, then iterate.
distractors: Correct: an average cannot exceed both of its constituent values.
Only one branch is guaranteed to preserve the expectation, not every branch to be optimal.
A union bound compares event probabilities and is not this conditional averaging identity.
A limit theorem is unnecessary for this exact finite identity.
teaching.takeaway: Derandomization follows a computable invariant rather than an appeal to typical outcomes.
teaching.followup: How would the argument change for a next bit with unequal probabilities?
teaching.tex: \max\{\mathbb E[W\mid h,0],\mathbb E[W\mid h,1]\}\ge\mathbb E[W\mid h].

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: In VC LP rounding, select vertices satisfying…
questions.why: Equality at 1/2 must be included to cover an edge with both endpoints at 1/2.
questions.readingLabel: Additional background: LP vertex-cover rounding

teaching.summary: The threshold must include equality. For any edge, the LP requires xᵤ+xᵥ≥1, so at least one endpoint has value at least one half. If equality were excluded, an edge with both endpoint values exactly one half would be left uncovered. This is a feasibility argument before the cost argument.
steps: Write the LP constraint for one arbitrary edge.
Use it to find an endpoint satisfying x≥1/2.
Include all such endpoints, including boundary values.
distractors: Strict inequality omits both endpoints when each equals one half.
Correct: the closed threshold guarantees every edge an included endpoint.
Restricting selection to value one can omit edges with two half-valued endpoints.
Selecting every positive coordinate is feasible but lacks the stated factor-two cost bound.
teaching.takeaway: Threshold boundaries are part of a feasibility proof.
teaching.followup: Why does selecting all positive LP variables fail the same simple factor-two cost comparison?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: Why is the rounded cover no more than twice the LP value?
questions.why: Sum the pointwise inequality over all vertices.
questions.readingLabel: Additional background: LP vertex-cover cost comparison

teaching.summary: For every selected vertex, xᵥ≥1/2, so its selection indicator one is at most 2xᵥ. For an unselected vertex the indicator is zero and the same inequality holds because xᵥ≥0. Summing these pointwise inequalities bounds the integral cover cost by twice the fractional value; nonnegative vertex weights can be included identically.
steps: Prove the indicator inequality separately for selected and unselected vertices.
Multiply by a nonnegative vertex cost if using the weighted model.
Sum, then compare the LP optimum with integral OPT by relaxation.
distractors: Counting edges does not establish the objective comparison on selected vertices.
Correct: summing a pointwise indicator bound gives the cost guarantee.
The relaxation can have fractional optima, which is why rounding is needed.
Regularity is not part of this proof.
teaching.takeaway: A local domination inequality can turn a feasibility threshold into a global approximation bound.
teaching.followup: Generalize the indicator inequality for a threshold τ>0.

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: Greedy weighted Set Cover picks…
options: The set covering most elements, regardless of cost
Minimum cost per newly covered element
questions.why: The key greedy criterion is cost divided by newly covered elements.
questions.readingLabel: Additional background: greedy weighted set cover; distinct from assigned primal–dual §7.1

teaching.summary: Greedy weighted set cover compares what a set costs with how many currently uncovered elements it newly covers. Previously covered elements must not appear in the denominator because they add no new progress. This ratio gives the equal per-element charge used in the harmonic analysis; it is a different algorithm from the assigned primal–dual set-cover method.
steps: Remove already covered elements from each candidate’s benefit count.
Compute cost divided by that remaining count.
Choose a minimum ratio and charge its newly covered elements equally.
distractors: Maximum uncovered count ignores potentially very large set costs.
Minimum set cost ignores how few new elements it covers.
Correct: cost per newly covered element measures the actual marginal price.
Choosing an uncovered element alone does not specify the greedy cost-benefit decision.
teaching.takeaway: A greedy rule needs a marginal benefit as well as a cost.
teaching.followup: Compare a cost-4 set covering eight new elements with a cost-1 set covering one new element.

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: What factor arises for a universe of n elements?
questions.why: The charging argument sums the harmonic series.
questions.readingLabel: Additional background: harmonic charging in greedy set cover

teaching.summary: During greedy covering, a remaining optimum set gives a benchmark for the cheapest available cost-per-new-element ratio. Summing the resulting per-element charges over successive remaining element counts creates the harmonic series Hₙ. The integral comparison Hₙ≤1+ln n turns this into the familiar logarithmic approximation bound.
steps: Charge each newly covered element the chosen set’s cost divided by its new coverage.
Compare each charge with an available optimum-set benchmark at that stage.
Sum reciprocal remaining counts to obtain a harmonic factor.
distractors: A square-root factor does not follow from the harmonic charging argument.
Correct: the bound is Hₙ, no more than one plus the natural logarithm of n.
Two is not the general greedy guarantee on unrestricted set systems.
Factorial growth is far larger than the harmonic charge sum.
teaching.takeaway: Recognize the sum generated by the charging proof instead of memorizing a theorem label.
teaching.followup: Why can the same proof be refined using a maximum relevant set size rather than the full universe in some formulations?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: In a primal–dual approximation proof, dual feasibility provides…
options: A lower bound for the minimization optimum
Automatic optimality of any primal solution
questions.why: Weak duality: any dual-feasible objective ≤ primal optimum for a minimization primal.
questions.readingLabel: W–S §7.1: dual lower bounds and cost charging

teaching.summary: For a minimization primal, any feasible dual objective is at most every feasible primal objective, hence at most OPT. An approximation proof uses this lower bound to pay for a constructed primal solution with a controlled multiplicative loss. Feasibility alone does not force complementary slackness or optimality.
steps: Check the direction of the primal optimization problem.
Apply weak duality to the exhibited feasible dual.
Supply a separate upper cost comparison for the algorithm’s feasible primal output.
distractors: Correct: a feasible dual certifies a lower bound on minimization OPT.
An arbitrary primal solution need not match the dual bound.
Dual feasibility is an objective certificate rather than a bit-length bound.
Randomness is not needed for weak duality.
teaching.takeaway: A lower bound is useful only with a proved link to the algorithm’s cost.
teaching.followup: What extra equalities would turn matching primal and dual certificates into an exact optimum?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: Why does raising dual variables not automatically guarantee a factor 2?
options: The factor requires a problem-specific charging bound
questions.why: One must bound how many times each dual increase is charged to selected primal objects.
questions.readingLabel: W–S §7.1 and §7.4: multiplicity controls the factor

teaching.summary: Increasing duals can establish a valid lower bound, but the returned primal solution can charge the same dual mass multiple times. The approximation ratio comes from bounding this charging multiplicity or an analogous problem-specific inequality. Different problems have different bounds, and even selected tight objects need cleanup or structure to control the total cost.
steps: Establish dual feasibility throughout growth.
Express selected cost through tightness or another explicit comparison.
Bound aggregate duplication before concluding a numerical approximation factor.
distractors: Dual variables need not be integers for weak duality or approximation.
Correct: the factor requires a separate structural cost-charge bound.
Graph optimization problems also satisfy LP weak duality.
A generic growth process does not force equality of primal and dual costs.
teaching.takeaway: Dual growth is a lower-bound mechanism, not an automatic universal factor-two theorem.
teaching.followup: Compare element frequency in set cover with aggregate active-component degree in Steiner forest.

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: Probability a random hyperplane separates unit vectors at angle θ is…
questions.why: Rotational symmetry gives exactly θ/π.
questions.readingLabel: W–S §§6.1–6.2: the angular separation calculation

teaching.summary: Project the random normal direction to the plane spanned by the two unit vectors. Rotational symmetry makes its direction uniform. The separating directions occupy total angular measure 2θ out of 2π, so the probability is θ/π. This differs from the SDP contribution (1−cos θ)/2, which must be compared rather than substituted.
steps: Reduce the separation event to the two-dimensional span of the endpoints.
Count the two separating angular sectors.
Normalize their combined angle 2θ by the full circle 2π.
distractors: Sine does not give the angular measure fraction; for θ=π it would incorrectly give zero.
Correct: θ/π equals the fraction of separating normal directions.
This is the relaxed edge objective, not the hyperplane separation probability.
Orthogonal vectors have probability one half, but other angles change it.
teaching.takeaway: Derive the random geometric event before comparing it to an optimization relaxation.
teaching.followup: Check the formula at equal, orthogonal, and opposite endpoint vectors.

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: The Goemans–Williamson ratio is approximately…
questions.why: The worst ratio θ/π divided by (1−cos θ)/2 is approximately 0.87856.
questions.readingLabel: W–S §§6.1–6.2: the uniform edgewise ratio

teaching.summary: The constant is the minimum over angles of rounded cut probability divided by relaxed edge value. For interior minimizers, differentiation gives 1−cos θ=θ sin θ; evaluating the minimum yields about 0.87856. Taking the minimum makes the edgewise inequality hold uniformly, allowing a nonnegative weighted sum and an approximation relative to integral OPT.
steps: Write the two per-edge expressions θ/π and (1−cos θ)/2.
Form their ratio and minimize over the admissible angular interval, with endpoint limits checked.
Sum the uniform comparison using nonnegative edge weights.
distractors: One half is the simple random-cut baseline rather than this SDP-rounding factor.
Approximately 0.632 is associated with a different exponential bound, not this angular minimum.
Correct: the worst angular ratio is approximately 0.87856.
A factor above one uses an incompatible maximization-guarantee convention here.
teaching.takeaway: An algorithm’s global factor comes from its worst admissible local ratio, not one favorable angle.
teaching.followup: Why does a negative edge weight break this edgewise summation proof?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: A dominating tree embedding satisfies…
questions.why: The sampled tree never underestimates original pairwise distances.
questions.readingLabel: W–S §§8.5–8.6: domination versus expected stretch

teaching.summary: A dominating embedding does not shorten original pairwise distances: every sampled tree has d_T(u,v)≥d(u,v). A separate theorem controls each pair’s expected expansion by O(log n). Domination alone permits very large distortion; expected expansion alone does not identify the largest realized stretch in one sampled tree.
steps: State the per-sample noncontraction condition.
Keep its inequality direction separate from the expected upper stretch bound.
Use the two conditions at their appropriate transfer steps.
distractors: This is contraction rather than domination.
Correct: sampled tree distances do not underestimate original distances.
Equality is a special isometric case, not a necessary property of dominating embeddings.
Zero distances cannot dominate positive original distances.
teaching.takeaway: A randomized embedding theorem has distinct deterministic and expected guarantees.
teaching.followup: Why does an MST of a cycle satisfy domination yet have a badly stretched pair?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: Why is Euclidean TSP PTAS geometry-specific?
options: Euclidean TSP is easy to solve exactly
Portal and boundary-crossing bounds use geometric dissections
It needs a complete bipartite graph
questions.why: Shifted dissections, portals and patching arguments rely on fixed-dimensional Euclidean structure.
questions.readingLabel: Additional background: Euclidean TSP §10.1; assigned §10.2 is planar MIS

teaching.summary: The Euclidean TSP scheme exploits fixed-dimensional geometric dissections, portals on cell boundaries, and patching estimates controlling crossings. Arbitrary metrics need not have these geometric structures, so the proof cannot be transferred simply because both problems use distances. The current assigned §10.2 concerns planar maximum independent set, a different structural scheme.
steps: Identify the dissection and portal structure used to restrict candidate tours.
Check where geometry bounds the cost of moving crossings and patching.
Keep this background scheme distinct from both general metric TSP and planar MIS.
distractors: The exact optimization problem remains computationally hard; the scheme approximates it.
Correct: portal and crossing estimates exploit Euclidean geometric structure.
Coordinates and distances need not all be integers.
Complete bipartiteness is not the structural hypothesis of this scheme.
teaching.takeaway: A PTAS often depends on a specific geometric or graph-structure theorem.
teaching.followup: Compare the role of portal restrictions here with deleting planar layer residues in Baker’s scheme.

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: For a MAX problem, YES OPT≥0.9m and NO OPT≤0.6m. What factor ρ would distinguish them via a ρ-approximation?
questions.why: On YES, output ≥ρ·0.9m; to exceed 0.6m need ρ>2/3. On NO, any feasible output ≤0.6m.
questions.readingLabel: W–S §§16.1,16.3: derive the NO-to-YES threshold

teaching.summary: Under the stated maximization convention, a YES input produces value at least 0.9ρm. A NO input has no feasible value above 0.6m. These ranges are strictly separated if 0.9ρ>0.6, so the threshold is ρ>2/3. Equality leaves a possible common boundary and does not guarantee a decision procedure.
steps: Translate the approximation guarantee into a YES output lower bound.
Use feasibility to bound every NO output from above.
Solve the strict comparison in the same ratio convention.
distractors: Correct: a factor above two thirds forces the YES lower output bound above the NO range.
The reversed inequality gives no such separation.
A guarantee of one tenth is too weak to exceed the NO threshold.
Arbitrarily small positive factors cannot distinguish these intervals.
teaching.takeaway: Hardness thresholds must retain completeness, soundness, and strictness explicitly.
teaching.followup: What does the distinguishing condition become if the algorithm’s guarantee is written ALG≥OPT/α?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: The PCP theorem can yield inapproximability because…
options: It creates constant-gap local constraint verification
It replaces all proofs by random assignments
questions.why: The constant local-verification gap translates to separated objective values.
questions.readingLabel: W–S §16.3: local tests become a gap instance

teaching.summary: A PCP verifier uses a random local test whose acceptance has a completeness–soundness gap. Enumerating polynomially many random tapes turns those tests into bounded-arity constraints on one common assignment to proof bits. The soundness gap survives only because the same proof is used for all tests; an exact decision reduction alone does not supply this quantitative gap.
steps: Track the verifier’s randomness and constant query count.
Create a local constraint for each random tape on the shared proof positions.
Translate completeness and soundness into separated optimum fractions.
distractors: The PCP construction does not prove P=NP.
Correct: a quantitative local-verification gap creates separated objective values.
PCP soundness does not make every LP relaxation integral.
The proof is specially encoded; it is not replaced by random assignments.
teaching.takeaway: A local test must enforce one global object to preserve a reduction’s soundness gap.
teaching.followup: Why would a separate satisfying assignment chosen independently for every test make the reduction useless?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: To prove B is NP-hard starting from NP-hard A, prove…
questions.why: The reduction must transform instances of the known-hard A into B.
questions.readingLabel: Related lecture: gap reductions; NP reductions are additional background.

teaching.summary: To establish hardness of B, use a solver for B to solve a known-hard problem A. The reduction must therefore take A-instances to B-instances, preserve YES and NO answers, and run in polynomial time. The reverse arrow would show A is no harder than B only if that reverse were actually A→B.
steps: Assume a polynomial-time algorithm for B as the hypothetical tool.
Map an instance x of A to f(x) of B with x∈A exactly when f(x)∈B.
Run the B algorithm on f(x). This would solve A, establishing the required hardness implication.
distractors: This direction uses an algorithm for A to solve B and does not establish B’s hardness from A’s.
Correct: A≤ₘᵖB lets a hypothetical efficient B solver solve the known-hard A.
Showing A lies in P would remove the intended known-hard starting point rather than transfer hardness.
Membership in coNP does not specify a reduction from the known-hard language.
teaching.takeaway: Read a reduction arrow as “an algorithm for the right side solves the left side.”
teaching.followup: State the two YES/NO objective thresholds needed when this becomes an approximation-gap reduction.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: Cook–Levin encodes…
questions.why: Local Boolean constraints represent a valid accepting nondeterministic computation.
questions.readingLabel: Related lecture: encoded computation tableaux; Cook–Levin is additional background.

teaching.summary: Cook–Levin records an accepting computation as a tableau: rows are configurations and local conditions verify legal transitions. The construction translates global machine acceptance into satisfiability of a polynomial-size formula. This is the finite precursor to the much longer tableaux checked locally in BFL.
steps: Choose a polynomial time bound for the nondeterministic computation.
Introduce Boolean variables describing tape symbols, states, and head positions at each time and location.
Require a legal start, locally valid transitions, and an accepting configuration; a satisfying assignment is an accepting tableau.
distractors: Scheduling job order is unrelated to the general encoding of a nondeterministic machine computation.
Correct: satisfying assignments describe valid accepting computation histories.
An LP dual certificate belongs to optimization and is not the object encoded by Cook–Levin.
Random graph thresholds concern probabilistic appearance, rather than encoding machine acceptance.
teaching.takeaway: A tableau turns a global computation into many local consistency constraints.
teaching.followup: Why does checking a long encoded tableau still require a consistency argument when different prover answers arrive on different queries?

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: Savitch’s theorem bounds NSPACE(s) by…
questions.why: A depth-O(s) midpoint recursion with O(s) space per level yields O(s²) space.
questions.readingLabel: Related lecture: depth-first space accounting; Savitch’s theorem is additional background.

teaching.summary: Savitch’s theorem gives a deterministic space bound, not a polynomial running-time guarantee. For space-constructible s(n)≥log n, reachability in the configuration graph can be decided by trying possible midpoint configurations recursively. Exponentially many trials can reuse the same working memory.
steps: A configuration uses O(s) bits, and the configuration graph has at most exponentially many vertices.
A midpoint recursion halves the candidate path length, giving O(s) recursion depth.
Each live frame stores O(s) bits of configurations and counters, so the total is O(s²) space.
distractors: Correct: under the standard constructibility and s≥log n conditions, nondeterministic space s is simulated in deterministic O(s²) space.
The recursion may revisit exponentially many midpoint candidates; its conclusion is about space, not this time bound.
The theorem does not make every polynomial-space computation polynomial-time.
O(log s) space does not even generally store one O(s)-bit configuration.
teaching.takeaway: A depth-first recomputation proof can trade a large amount of time for a small live stack.
teaching.followup: List the data held by one midpoint-recursion frame and explain why completed branches need not stay in memory.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: Why does TQBF lie in PSPACE?
questions.why: Depth-first recursion over polynomially many quantifiers uses polynomial working memory.
questions.readingLabel: Related lecture: quantified formulas and polynomial-space evaluation.

teaching.summary: A quantified formula may require visiting exponentially many assignments, but a depth-first evaluator stores only the current assignment prefix and the values of unfinished recursive calls. Universal quantifiers require both branches and existential quantifiers require one successful branch; neither forces all branches to coexist in memory.
steps: Maintain the values of at most polynomially many quantified variables along the current recursion path.
Evaluate the two choices of the next variable one after another, reusing space between them.
Combine branch values according to the quantifier and return a single Boolean result to the preceding frame.
distractors: A small-circuit claim is unnecessary and does not follow from the definition of a quantified formula.
Correct: the recursion has polynomial depth and stores polynomial-size current information.
A formula can have exponentially many assignments; enumerating them does not give polynomial time.
TQBF explicitly permits universal quantifiers, whose two branches are evaluated with space reuse.
teaching.takeaway: Exponential search can remain in PSPACE when its branches are explored sequentially.
teaching.followup: Explain the space needed for an alternating string of n quantifiers without claiming that its evaluation is polynomial-time.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: In RP on a NO instance, the acceptance probability is…
questions.why: RP allows no false positives.
questions.readingLabel: Related lecture: error conventions; RP is additional background.

teaching.summary: RP has one-sided error: it never accepts a NO instance, and accepts a YES instance with probability at least a fixed positive constant, conventionally 1/2. Keeping the allowed error side explicit prevents confusing RP with coRP or BPP.
steps: Fix an input outside the language and quantify over all random strings.
For RP, none of those strings may cause acceptance, so the acceptance probability is zero.
On a YES input, at least half the random choices accept under the chosen standard convention.
distractors: Correct: RP has no false positives, so NO-instance acceptance is exactly zero.
At least one half is the lower bound on YES-instance acceptance, not on NO instances.
A positive false-acceptance probability is allowed in BPP’s two-sided convention, not in RP.
Certain acceptance on a NO instance contradicts the definition of recognition.
teaching.takeaway: State the input type and the error side before applying an amplification rule.
teaching.followup: Reverse the permitted error side and formulate the corresponding coRP condition.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: For k≥1 independent RP trials, each with YES success probability at least 1/2, what is the sharpest listed bound on failure when accepting if any trial succeeds?
questions.why: All k independent trials must fail; each does so with probability at most 1/2.
questions.readingLabel: Related lecture: error amplification; RP is additional background.

teaching.summary: With OR repetition, a YES instance is missed only if every independent trial rejects. Each trial rejects with probability at most 1/2. NO instances remain rejected with certainty because no individual RP trial can accept them.
steps: Run k independent copies on the same input using fresh random strings.
Accept if any copy accepts; failure on a YES input is the intersection of all k rejection events.
Multiply the independent failure bounds to obtain at most (1/2)^k=2⁻ᵏ.
distractors: 1/k decays much more slowly and is not the direct product bound from independent trials.
This bounds the probability that at least one trial succeeds, rather than that every trial fails.
Correct: all k independent failures are necessary for OR repetition to miss a YES instance.
A fixed one-third error does not reflect the improvement from increasing k.
teaching.takeaway: Choose AND or OR repetition to preserve the correct one-sided error convention.
teaching.followup: What changes if the k runs reuse the same random string?

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: For a nonzero polynomial of total degree at most 3 over F₁₀₁, sampled at independent uniform field coordinates, the probability of evaluating to zero is at most…
questions.why: Schwartz–Zippel gives degree/field-size.
questions.readingLabel: Lecture: fixed polynomial, fresh random evaluation, and the root bound.

teaching.summary: A false-zero event occurs when a nonzero polynomial evaluates to zero, so the evaluation fails to reveal nonidentity. Schwartz–Zippel bounds this event by total degree divided by the size of the uniformly sampled coordinate set. It is an upper bound and need not be attained.
steps: Check that the polynomial is nonzero over F₁₀₁ and has total degree three.
Sample each coordinate independently and uniformly from the field.
Apply the total-degree bound: false-zero probability is at most 3/101.
distractors: Correct: total degree three divided by 101 gives the stated false-zero upper bound.
The reciprocal of the degree is not the Schwartz–Zippel probability formula.
This is a lower bound on detecting nonzeroness, the complement of the failure upper bound.
A nonzero polynomial can have roots, so a randomized identity test can miss it.
teaching.takeaway: Specify whether “error” means a false zero or a detected nonzero before taking complements.
teaching.followup: Find a univariate degree-three polynomial over F₁₀₁ with three distinct roots.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: Which issue can invalidate a useful polynomial identity test?
options: Choosing the field much larger than degree
Letting polynomial degree grow comparable to field size
questions.why: Error bound d/|F| is uninformative when d is too large.
questions.readingLabel: Lecture: degree growth and the field-size soundness budget.

teaching.summary: A root-counting bound is useful only if the degree is small compared with the sampling set. Naive quantified arithmetization can create huge degrees, which is why the protocol needs degree control in addition to finite-field arithmetic.
steps: Write the error estimate as d/|F| and include all rounds if the check is interactive.
If d is comparable with |F|, the estimate can be a constant near one or worse.
A nonzero formal polynomial such as X^|F|−X vanishes at every field element, demonstrating the danger of large degrees.
distractors: A larger field relative to fixed degree improves the error estimate.
Correct: degree comparable to field size can destroy the useful gap between truth and cheating.
Independent uniform sampling is a standard hypothesis supporting, rather than invalidating, the bound.
Finite fields are a valid setting when the polynomial and sampling assumptions are respected.
teaching.takeaway: Degree reduction is part of soundness, not merely a convenient representation change.
teaching.followup: Compute the degree and evaluation behavior of X^p−X over the prime field F_p.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: The first sum-check verification is…
questions.why: The initial claimed Boolean sum is partitioned by the first variable.
questions.readingLabel: Lecture: sum-check’s endpoint identity before the random challenge.

teaching.summary: The first round polynomial sums the target function over all but the first Boolean variable. Its two endpoint values partition the claimed full sum according to that variable being 0 or 1. This identity is checked before choosing the next random field point.
steps: Define h₁(X) as the sum over all remaining Boolean coordinates.
Separate the original Boolean cube into the two disjoint slices x₁=0 and x₁=1.
Add the slice sums to recover the initial claimed total H.
distractors: Correct: the two endpoint sums cover the entire original Boolean domain exactly once.
The x₁=1 slice omits all inputs with x₁=0.
A Boolean sum splits additively, rather than as a product of the two slice sums.
The honest restriction can depend nontrivially on X, so constancy is not required.
teaching.takeaway: Each sum-check consistency identity comes from a partition of the remaining sum.
teaching.followup: Write the analogous endpoint identity in round two after the first variable has been fixed randomly.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: For g(x,y)=xy+2x+y over F₁₇, ∑_{x,y∈{0,1}} g(x,y) is…
questions.why: Values are 0,1,2,4; their sum is 7.
questions.readingLabel: Lecture: work a Boolean sum before verifying it algebraically.

teaching.summary: The four Boolean inputs are (0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1). Their values are 0,1,2,4, so the integer sum is 7 and its field residue in F₁₇ is also 7. Enumerating this tiny example clarifies what the protocol’s claimed sum represents.
steps: Compute the values on each Boolean pair without replacing a sum by a field-wide enumeration.
Add 0+1+2+4 to obtain 7.
Reduce modulo 17 only if needed; here 7 already lies in the standard residue range.
distractors: This omits part of the linear-term contribution across the four Boolean inputs.
This misses one unit of the xy contribution or miscounts a slice.
Correct: all four values sum to 7, unchanged modulo 17.
This overcounts the constant or linear contributions; direct evaluation gives only 7.
teaching.takeaway: The Boolean summation domain and the finite field of arithmetic play different roles.
teaching.followup: Derive the honest first-round polynomial h₁(X)=Σ_y g(X,y) and check its endpoint sum.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: For sum-check with k variables of individual degree at most d, which expression is the usual degree-based union-bound error estimate before capping it at 1?
questions.why: Each dishonest round escapes a random check with probability ≤d/|F|; union bound.
questions.readingLabel: Lecture: conditional root errors and the final direct evaluation.

teaching.summary: For a false initial sum to reach an accepted correct final evaluation, some round must accidentally replace a false claim by a true one. Conditional on the preceding transcript, the dishonest and honest round polynomials differ and have degree at most d. The union bound adds their root-agreement probabilities.
steps: Fix the polynomial message before the round’s fresh random field challenge.
Apply the degree-d root bound to the nonzero difference, giving at most d/|F| for that round.
Union-bound the possible first repairs over k rounds to obtain at most kd/|F|.
distractors: Correct: k opportunities each have a conditional degree-to-field-size error bound.
A larger field should reduce error; this expression instead grows with field size.
Degree alone does not produce exponential soundness decay in this protocol.
This grows with field size and does not represent a useful root-error probability.
teaching.takeaway: Round count belongs in the total soundness estimate even when every individual check is low degree.
teaching.followup: Replace the common degree d by per-round bounds d₁,…,d_k and state the resulting estimate.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: When evaluating an IP protocol tree in polynomial space, prover turns correspond to…
questions.why: The optimal prover chooses the next message to maximize acceptance probability.
questions.readingLabel: Lecture: legal prover maximization over compatible hidden verifier tapes.

teaching.summary: A prover tries to maximize acceptance, but its reply can depend only on its visible history. With private verifier coins, all hidden tapes compatible with that history must share the same selected reply. Maximize over legal replies outside the average over those tapes.
steps: Group verifier random tapes that give the same visible prover transcript.
For each possible reply, calculate its weighted continuation acceptance over that information set.
Choose one reply achieving the largest weighted value; do not choose separately for each hidden tape.
distractors: The prover is strategic, so averaging over its replies does not compute its optimal value.
Correct, with the essential qualification that each choice respects the prover’s information set.
Sampling one arbitrary reply need not achieve or compute the best legal strategy.
The protocol’s fixed verifier is not universally quantified at a prover node in this optimization.
teaching.takeaway: The optimization variable is a legal message based on the visible transcript.
teaching.followup: Give the two-hidden-tape example where moving the maximum inside the average changes 1/2 into 1.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: Why does traversing an exponential interaction tree use only polynomial space?
options: The tree has polynomially many nodes
Depth-first recursion stores one polynomial-length history per level
PSPACE machines can store the whole tree
questions.why: Depth and size of each history are polynomial, so DFS uses polynomial space.
questions.readingLabel: Lecture: recomputation and polynomial-space evaluation.

teaching.summary: The interaction tree can have exponentially many nodes, while its depth and every transcript length remain polynomial. Depth-first traversal stores one active branch and enough counters to enumerate alternatives. Private randomness additionally requires grouping compatible tapes without storing their entire list.
steps: Bound the number of simultaneously live recursion levels by the polynomial protocol length.
At each level keep a polynomial-size visible history, loop counters, and a probability accumulator.
Recompute completed branches or tape compatibility when needed, trading extra time for limited live memory.
distractors: The tree can be exponential; the proof is precisely that its entire size need not fit in memory.
Correct: polynomial depth and polynomial-size frames yield polynomial live storage.
The verifier’s computation and memory are bounded; infinite memory is not part of the model.
A PSPACE simulation stores a traversal stack, not all nodes of an exponential tree.
teaching.takeaway: A polynomial-space argument must justify both the recursion stack and the size of its arithmetic.
teaching.followup: Explain how an acceptance numerator can require polynomial bits despite exponentially many random tapes.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: What is a core obstruction in naive arithmetization of QBF?
options: Quantifiers cannot be evaluated on 0 and 1
questions.why: Degree reduction/multilinearization is crucial to maintain a polynomial degree bound.
questions.readingLabel: Lecture: quantifier products and controlled-degree arithmetization.

teaching.summary: Arithmetizing Boolean operations is easy on individual 0/1 inputs. The obstacle is that quantifier elimination can multiply two restrictions of the current polynomial, increasing degrees in the surviving variables. Repetition without a reduction schedule can make those degrees exponential.
steps: Represent universal elimination by a product of the two Boolean restrictions.
A product can double the degree of each still-free variable.
Insert and verify degree-reduction operations so every message and root-error budget remains polynomial.
distractors: Finite fields exist; the question is choosing one compatible with controlled degrees and error.
Correct: uncontrolled degree growth defeats the polynomial-size protocol and its useful root bound.
The 0/1 restrictions are well-defined and supply the basic quantifier identities.
TQBF is a standard PSPACE-complete problem and is the intended starting point.
teaching.takeaway: A correct Boolean encoding is only the beginning; control its behavior away from the cube.
teaching.followup: Find a polynomial that agrees with X on {0,1} but has arbitrarily large formal degree.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: In arithmetization on Boolean inputs, OR(x,y) can be represented by…
questions.why: x+y−xy equals logical OR for Boolean x,y.
questions.readingLabel: Lecture: verify Boolean connective polynomials on their intended domain.

teaching.summary: The OR polynomial x+y−xy equals 0 only at (0,0) and equals 1 at the other three Boolean pairs. It is an encoding on the Boolean cube; away from that cube it is simply a field polynomial, not a truth-value operation.
steps: Evaluate at (0,0) to get zero.
If exactly one input is 1, the product term is zero and the sum is one.
At (1,1), subtract the duplicate contribution: 1+1−1=1.
distractors: xy represents AND on Boolean inputs, since it is 1 only when both are 1.
1−x represents NOT x and ignores y; at (0,0) it gives 1 even though OR must give 0.
Correct: subtracting xy repairs the double-counting of the both-true case.
x−y gives different values when the inputs are exchanged and is not Boolean OR.
teaching.takeaway: Verify the truth table first, then separately analyze the polynomial’s degree.
teaching.followup: Use the OR identity to derive the existential-quantifier operator on two restrictions.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: What is the essential restriction on classical MIP provers?
options: They cannot communicate after receiving their questions
questions.why: The no-communication condition enables cross-checking of correlated answers.
questions.readingLabel: Lecture: isolated provers, local response functions, and consistency.

teaching.summary: Classical provers can be computationally unbounded and can agree on their strategies or share randomness beforehand. During a round, each response must depend only on that prover’s own question and earlier local information. This isolation lets the verifier compare answers against one fixed response function.
steps: Allow advance coordination, then fix a shared seed to obtain deterministic local strategies for analysis.
Give the provers separate questions and forbid communication after those questions arrive.
Use one prover’s index-only answer to constrain another prover’s larger proposed view.
distractors: Their computational power is not the restriction that creates the consistency mechanism.
Correct: isolation after questions prevents tailoring an answer to the other prover’s full question.
Advance coordination is allowed and must be handled in the soundness analysis.
Entanglement changes the model and is not the classical BFL setting stated in this question.
teaching.takeaway: No communication is an information restriction, not a computational limitation.
teaching.followup: Why does sending the first prover’s whole view to the second destroy the fixed-oracle argument?

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: For classical (non-entangled) provers, MIP equals…
questions.why: The classical multi-prover theorem is MIP=NEXP.
questions.readingLabel: Lecture: the two containments of classical MIP = NEXP.

teaching.summary: BFL’s theorem concerns classical isolated provers. The upper bound guesses exponentially long deterministic response tables and evaluates the verifier. The harder reverse containment checks an algebraic encoding of an exponentially long computation using short local questions.
steps: For MIP⊆NEXP, bound the length of the response tables and the time to enumerate verifier coins.
For NEXP⊆MIP, combine encoded computation, isolation-based consistency, and robust algebraic testing.
Keep the model classical: a different prover correlation model needs a separate theorem and soundness proof.
distractors: NP is already verifiable by simpler witness systems, but is not the full classical multi-prover characterization.
PSPACE characterizes single-prover polynomial-time interaction, not this classical isolated multi-prover model.
Correct: the two BFL containments identify classical MIP with NEXP.
The response-table upper bound gives nondeterministic exponential time, not this larger space characterization.
teaching.takeaway: A class equality packages two different proofs; knowing its name does not prove either inclusion.
teaching.followup: Which part of the NEXP lower-bound protocol needs the robust multilinearity theorem as a substantive input?

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: Perfect zero knowledge requires simulator and real view distributions to be…
options: Equivalent only in their final bit
questions.why: Perfect ZK requires distributional equality of the verifier’s entire view.
questions.readingLabel: Lecture: perfect, statistical, and computational comparisons of full views.

teaching.summary: Perfect zero knowledge asks for exact equality of the simulator’s output distribution and the prescribed real verifier view. Statistical zero knowledge permits a negligible statistical distance; computational zero knowledge permits indistinguishability against efficient tests. Comparing only the final output bit is weaker than all three.
steps: Specify the complete view being simulated, including its required messages, randomness, and auxiliary input.
For perfect zero knowledge, assign exactly the same probability to every possible view.
Do not replace equality by approximate distance or by agreement of one projection such as acceptance.
distractors: Computational indistinguishability is a weaker comparison and does not require exact equality.
Correct: perfect zero knowledge requires identical full-view distributions.
A fixed positive distance such as 0.1 is not equality and is not a negligible-error guarantee.
Matching a final bit can leave all transcript information different and even leak a witness-dependent value.
teaching.takeaway: The strength of zero knowledge is defined by how the entire distributions are compared.
teaching.followup: Give two full-view distributions with identical acceptance probability but different supports.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: For full zero knowledge, the simulator quantifies over…
questions.why: Full ZK protects against arbitrary efficient (possibly malicious) verifiers.
questions.readingLabel: Lecture: malicious-verifier quantifiers and the simulator’s efficiency.

teaching.summary: Full zero knowledge protects against every efficient verifier strategy in the stated model, including malicious challenges and auxiliary information. For each such verifier, there must be a suitable efficient simulator. The existence of one simulator only for the honest verifier proves a different, weaker statement.
steps: Choose an arbitrary polynomial-time verifier V*, not only the protocol’s prescribed verifier.
Supply a simulator for that V* under the required running-time and auxiliary-input conventions.
Compare its simulated full view with the real interaction on true statements using the theorem’s chosen notion.
distractors: This is the honest-verifier variant and omits malicious strategies.
Correct: the full definition quantifies over all efficient verifier strategies, with an appropriate simulator for each.
Cheating provers appear in soundness; zero knowledge is about what verifiers can learn.
The standard efficient-verifier definition does not require simulation for every unbounded verifier.
teaching.takeaway: Write “for every verifier, there exists a simulator” before analyzing an example.
teaching.followup: Why can a simulator for a uniform challenge fail when the verifier chooses its challenge based on the first message?

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: Toda’s theorem says…
questions.why: Toda established that counting-oracle polynomial time contains the polynomial hierarchy.
questions.readingLabel: Lecture: Toda’s counting-oracle containment and LFKN consequences.

teaching.summary: Toda’s theorem puts every fixed level of the polynomial hierarchy within deterministic polynomial-time computation with a counting oracle. It is a containment theorem. Combining it with an appropriate interactive simulation requires additional protocol composition and error budgeting.
steps: Interpret P^#P as polynomial-time oracle computation with the relevant counting power.
Read the theorem in its given direction: each language in PH has such an oracle computation.
Keep the reverse containment or equality with a hierarchy level as separate claims, not part of this statement.
distractors: Correct: this is the hierarchy-to-counting-oracle containment used in the consequence chain.
The theorem does not collapse the hierarchy to NP.
This is a reverse containment and is not the statement of Toda’s theorem.
The theorem uses a counting oracle; removing it would be a much stronger unsupported conclusion.
teaching.takeaway: A powerful oracle containment does not itself eliminate the oracle or collapse the hierarchy.
teaching.followup: Explain which separate LFKN-style ingredient is needed to turn a counting-oracle computation into an interactive proof.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: What does the 0–1 permanent count?
options: Perfect matchings in a bipartite graph
questions.why: Each permutation contribution 1 corresponds to a perfect matching.
questions.readingLabel: Lecture: permanent as a matching count and a verifiable algebraic claim.

teaching.summary: A permutation selects one column for every row and uses every column once. For a 0–1 adjacency matrix of a bipartite graph, its product is 1 exactly when all selected row–column edges exist. Summing without signs therefore counts its perfect matchings.
steps: Regard rows as left vertices and columns as right vertices.
Identify each permutation with a candidate matching using every vertex exactly once.
A missing edge makes that product zero; every present perfect matching contributes one.
distractors: Independent sets have no requirement to match every left vertex to a unique right vertex.
Correct: exactly the feasible permutation products correspond to bipartite perfect matchings.
Triangle counts require triples of mutually adjacent vertices and use a different expression.
Spanning forests permit several tree components and are not encoded by one permutation per row.
teaching.takeaway: The permanent resembles a determinant but omits the alternating signs that can cancel matchings.
teaching.followup: Compute the permanent and determinant of the all-ones 2×2 matrix and explain their difference.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: The constant-round Arthur–Merlin hierarchy collapse states…
questions.why: Constant public-coin rounds can be compressed to two AM messages, with standard conventions.
questions.readingLabel: Related lecture: class containments versus round conventions; AM is additional background.

teaching.summary: The constant-round Arthur–Merlin hierarchy collapses to its two-message public-coin form under the standard conventions and bounded-error amplification. The number of rounds must be a fixed constant; this does not compress arbitrary polynomial-round interaction or imply collapse of PH.
steps: Fix the AM convention, including which party speaks first and how messages are counted.
Keep k constant independent of input length in the round-collapse theorem.
Conclude equality with AM[2] under those conventions, not with unrelated proof-system classes.
distractors: The public-coin round collapse is not a theorem that the entire polynomial hierarchy equals AM.
Correct: the theorem compresses any fixed constant number of AM messages to the standard two-message class.
No equality of NP and coNP follows from the public-coin message-compression statement.
Multiple isolated provers are a different model from a single public-coin prover.
teaching.takeaway: “Constant-round” is a quantitative hypothesis, and the meaning of “round” must be fixed.
teaching.followup: Why would substituting k=n into this theorem change its hypothesis rather than give the same conclusion?

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: Which upper bound is standard for AM?
questions.why: AM is contained in Π₂ᵖ. This does not collapse PH.
questions.readingLabel: Related lecture: disciplined class containments; the AM upper bound is additional background.

teaching.summary: Under standard polynomial-time public-coin bounded-error conventions, AM is contained in the second universal level of the polynomial hierarchy. This theorem has its own amplification and quantifier argument. It should not be inferred merely from the fact that Arthur samples randomness.
steps: Fix the standard two-message AM class and its completeness and soundness constants.
Invoke the established AM⊆Π₂ᵖ containment with those conventions.
Do not replace that upper bound by deterministic polynomial time, logspace, or coNP without an additional theorem.
distractors: Correct: Π₂ᵖ is the standard hierarchy upper bound under the stated conventions.
AM⊆P is a stronger statement than the known bound used here.
Logspace is a much stronger upper bound and is not supplied by public-coin verification.
The standard Π₂ᵖ upper bound does not by itself place AM in coNP.
teaching.takeaway: Know what a class containment states, but keep its proof separate from its name.
teaching.followup: State the quantifier order defining Π₂ᵖ and identify the extra argument needed to encode AM into it.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: NP=PCP(O(log n),O(1)) means…
options: O(log n) random bits, O(1) proof queries
O(1) random bits and O(log n) proof queries
questions.why: The two parameters count verifier randomness and accessed proof positions.
questions.readingLabel: Related lecture: PCP gaps; the verifier-parameter definition is foundational background.

teaching.summary: The two PCP parameters count random bits and queried proof positions, not proof length. O(log n) random bits permit polynomially many random seeds, while O(1) queries let a reduction form constant-arity local constraints. The usual statement includes constant completeness–soundness separation.
steps: The verifier runs in polynomial time and receives query access to an encoded proof.
Its random tape length is O(log n), and on one run it reads only O(1) proof symbols.
The gap between honest acceptance and false-instance acceptance supplies the objective gap in PCP-based reductions.
distractors: The first parameter is the random-bit budget, not the total proof length.
Correct: the parameters measure verifier randomness and the number of accessed proof positions.
This swaps the two resources, changing the meaning of the theorem.
The standard PCP theorem allows bounded soundness error strictly below completeness.
teaching.takeaway: Locality concerns how much of an encoded proof is read on one run.
teaching.followup: Explain why O(log n) random bits allow a polynomial-size family of local constraints in a gap reduction.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: PCP proofs differ from raw NP witnesses because…
options: They are specially encoded for local testability
They consist only of the input
questions.why: A PCP uses an encoding with robust locally detectable constraint violations.
questions.readingLabel: Related lecture: locally checkable encodings and gap soundness.

teaching.summary: A raw NP witness may encode validity in a way that requires inspecting much of the witness. A PCP re-encodes the information so that a false input forces a noticeable fraction of local checks to reject, even against an adversarial proof string. This robust global-to-local property is the key distinction.
steps: Begin with a witness whose global correctness is a polynomial-time predicate.
Encode it and design local checks that accept valid encodings with the required completeness.
Prove soundness for every alleged proof string, including inconsistent or badly encoded strings.
distractors: Correct: robust local testability is the purpose of the specialized proof encoding.
In the standard theorem the relevant proof length can be polynomial; locality does not prohibit that.
Uniqueness is not required, and multiple witnesses or valid encodings may exist.
The proof carries witness-related information beyond the public input.
teaching.takeaway: A local verifier needs a global soundness theorem, not just locally meaningful tests.
teaching.followup: Compare this requirement with the robust global-polynomial conclusion needed in BFL multilinearity testing.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: Which inequality proves an outcome with no bad events from a nonnegative integer-valued bad-event count X?
questions.why: If X≥1 for every outcome, then E[X]≥1; contrapositive.
questions.readingLabel: Additional reference lesson: First moment

teaching.summary: For a nonnegative integer-valued count, absence of the zero outcome would force the count to be at least one everywhere. An expectation below one contradicts that possibility and therefore certifies at least one outcome with no bad objects.
steps: State nonnegativity and integrality; a positive value must then be at least one.
If Pr(X=0)=0, averaging X≥1 gives E[X]≥1.
Take the contrapositive: E[X]<1 forces positive probability of X=0, hence existence of a good outcome.
distractors: This is the strict expectation threshold that excludes an everywhere-positive integer bad count.
A large expectation gives no guarantee of a zero outcome.
A constant variable equal to one has variance zero but no good outcome.
A large second moment does not imply a zero outcome.
teaching.takeaway: An expectation argument gives existence, not necessarily an efficient search procedure.
teaching.followup: Why does a non-integer variable constantly equal to one-half invalidate the same reasoning?

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: For a fixed k-vertex subset of Kₙ with k≥2, what is the probability of a monochromatic Kₖ under independent fair edge colors?
questions.why: All C(k,2) edges must be red or all blue: two choices, each probability 2^{-C(k,2)}.
questions.readingLabel: Additional reference lesson: First moment and Ramsey counting

teaching.summary: The candidate clique has one independent random color per edge. To be monochromatic, all its edges must receive one prescribed color, and the all-red and all-blue cases are disjoint when there is at least one edge.
steps: A k-vertex clique has C(k,2) edges; the number of vertices is not the number of independent color choices.
For k≥2, all-red has probability 2^−C(k,2), and all-blue has the same probability.
Add the disjoint alternatives to obtain 2·2^−C(k,2)=2^{1−C(k,2)}.
distractors: This confuses the k vertices with the C(k,2) independently colored edges.
Two disjoint monochromatic colors each contribute 2^−C(k,2).
The ambient graph size n does not determine the event on this fixed clique.
One-half holds for some very small cases, not for general k.
teaching.takeaway: Count the independent random choices that determine the fixed event before multiplying by the number of candidates.

Correct: charge B−1 sufficiently full bins to total volume.
teaching.takeaway: State which exceptional bin creates the additive term.
teaching.followup: What changes if small items are allowed size greater than ε?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: Linear grouping rounds some large item sizes upward. Why is feasibility of a packing of rounded items easy to transfer back to the represented original items?
options: Original items are no larger than their rounded representatives
Upward rounding never changes the optimum
The number of items falls to one
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: Replacing a rounded item by a no-larger original cannot increase any bin load, so the same grouping of items remains feasible. This proves only the transfer of a rounded solution back to the original input. Bounding how many bins the rounded instance needs is a different argument, using grouping shifts and separate treatment of the exceptional group.
steps: Check the size comparison for each original and its rounded representative.
Apply that comparison separately inside each bin’s capacity inequality.
Keep the cost comparison to the original optimum as an additional proof obligation.
distractors: Correct: a coordinatewise decrease preserves each bin’s capacity constraint.
Upward rounding can increase the optimum, so grouping analysis is still needed.
Feasibility does not require every bin to be full.
Grouping reduces the number of types, not the item count to one.
teaching.takeaway: Feasibility transfer and optimum comparison are distinct directions of a rounding proof.
teaching.followup: Which implication reverses if sizes are rounded downward?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: A clause of weight 16 has four distinct literals on different variables and contains no complementary pair. Under independent fair truth assignments, what is its expected contribution?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Worked example and its approximation accounting

teaching.summary: Only the one truth pattern falsifying all four literals makes the clause fail. Its failure probability is 1/16, so the weight-16 clause contributes 16·15/16=15 in expectation. Clause indicators may be dependent across clauses; their weighted expectations can still be summed by linearity.
steps: Each of the four literals is false independently with probability one half.
Multiply to get clause failure probability (1/2)^4=1/16.
Multiply satisfaction probability 15/16 by weight 16.
distractors: Fourteen uses the three-literal satisfaction probability.
Correct: a four-literal clause has expected weighted contribution fifteen.
Eight uses the one-literal satisfaction probability.
Twelve uses the two-literal satisfaction probability.
teaching.takeaway: Literal independence is used inside a clause; linearity sums clauses without inter-clause independence.
teaching.followup: What changes if the clause contains both x and its negation?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: After fixing some variables, the two conditional expected objective values for the next fair bit are 12 and 18. Which deterministic choice preserves the current conditional expectation?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: Before fixing this bit the conditional expectation is the average (12+18)/2=15. The branch of value 18 is at least that average and therefore preserves the lower-bound invariant. Repeating this choice eventually produces a deterministic assignment whose actual objective is at least the starting expectation, provided the conditional expectations are computable.
steps: Partition the current conditional distribution by the next bit.
Apply the tower property to identify the current value as 15.
Choose the branch valued 18 and continue with the same invariant.
distractors: The averaging identity itself supplies a deterministic nondecreasing choice.
The stated values are unequal, and twelve is below their mean.
Correct: eighteen is at least the current conditional expectation fifteen.
Twelve decreases the maintained lower bound from fifteen.
teaching.takeaway: Conditional expectation derandomizes an efficiently computable lower-bound invariant.
teaching.followup: For a biased next bit with probabilities 1/4 and 3/4, what averaging equation replaces the simple mean?
teaching.tex: \mathbb E[W\mid h]=\tfrac12\mathbb E[W\mid h,0]+\tfrac12\mathbb E[W\mid h,1].

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: A fair assignment is applied to the written clause (x∨x). What is its satisfaction probability?
options: 1/4, because both copies must be true
1/2, because the two literal events coincide
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Limits and changed assumptions

teaching.summary: The clause is equivalent to the single literal x. Repeating the same variable does not create independent literal events, so the distinct-variable formula 1−2^−k cannot use the written length two here. Simplifying repetitions before applying the standard clause calculation makes the hypothesis explicit.
steps: Rewrite x∨x as x by Boolean idempotence.
Observe that both copies are false on exactly the same half of assignments.
Apply the one-distinct-literal probability one half.
distractors: OR needs at least one true copy, and both copies already coincide.
Three quarters treats repeated copies as independent events.
Repetition is not a complementary literal pair and does not make a tautology.
Correct: the clause is true exactly when x is true.
teaching.takeaway: Count independent distinct variables, not repeated syntax.
teaching.followup: Compare this clause with (x∨¬x) and identify why that case is always satisfied.

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: For the positive clause x∨y, independently round x true with probability 0.2 and y true with probability 0.3. If its LP clause value is z=0.5, what is satisfaction probability divided by z?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Worked example and its approximation accounting

teaching.summary: Both literals fail with probability 0.8·0.7=0.56, so the actual success probability is 0.44. Dividing by the fractional clause value 0.5 gives 0.88. The LP clause value is a benchmark, not itself a probability produced by independent rounding.
steps: Compute failure using independence across the two variables.
Subtract from one to obtain success probability 0.44.
Normalize by the LP contribution z=0.5 to get 0.88.
distractors: This reverses or miscomputes the normalization.
This is the unnormalized satisfaction probability rather than the requested ratio.
The LP value is a benchmark and is not the requested normalized success.
teaching.takeaway: Compare rounded expectation with the fractional objective term by term.
teaching.followup: How does the failure product change if the clause is x∨¬y?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: For a unit clause with LP value z=1, fair assignment satisfies it with probability 1/2 and LP-marginal rounding with probability 1. What exact satisfaction probability does their equal mixture give for this clause?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: An equal mixture chooses one of the two assignment procedures with probability one half. Its clause contribution is therefore the average of their expectations, namely 3/4. This clause calculation is part of an analysis that must hold for every clause length; checking only unit clauses does not by itself prove the complete MAX-SAT ratio.
steps: Write the mixture expectation as half of each procedure’s expectation.
Verify other clause lengths separately before summing weighted contributions.
distractors: One would require always using the LP branch in this example.
Correct: the mixture expectation is three quarters.
One half ignores the better LP-rounding branch.
Two thirds is not the expectation of this specified equal mixture.
teaching.takeaway: A mixture averages guarantees; taking the better realized solution can only improve that average.
teaching.followup: Why can the better of two produced assignments be used instead of explicitly sampling which output to keep?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: A clause contains ¬x and y. LP truth marginals are x=0.8, y=0.1. Under independent marginal rounding, which clause-failure probability is correct?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Limits and changed assumptions

teaching.summary: The literal ¬x is false exactly when x is true, with probability 0.8; y is false with probability 0.9. Different variables are rounded independently, giving failure 0.72 and success 0.28. Literal polarity must be translated before using the generic product of failure probabilities.
steps: Translate the negated literal’s failure event into x=true.
