Translate the positive literal’s failure event into y=false.
Multiply 0.8 and 0.9, using independence across x and y.
distractors: This uses the probability that y is true rather than false.
Both factors describe the wrong literal events for simultaneous failure.
Correct: both factors describe literal falsity, not variable truth uniformly.
This uses the probability that ¬x is true in a failure product.
teaching.takeaway: Write truth and falsity marginals for each literal before applying AM–GM or a product bound.
teaching.followup: What happens to this computation if both written literals use the same variable?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: A threshold α is uniform on [1/2,1]. What is E[1/α], the quantity arising in a threshold tree-cost bound?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: The density is two on an interval of length one half, so the expectation integrates 2/α from one half to one and equals 2 ln 2. It is not 1/E[α]=4/3. A randomized threshold analysis must average the actual nonlinear cost coefficient rather than substitute the mean threshold.
steps: Normalize the uniform density to 2 on [1/2,1].
Integrate 2∫(1/α)dα across that interval.
Evaluate 2(ln 1−ln(1/2))=2 ln 2.
distractors: Two is its maximum value, not its mean.
Four thirds is the reciprocal of the mean threshold, a different expression.
Log two omits the uniform density factor two.
Correct: the coefficient’s expectation is two log two.
teaching.takeaway: Nonlinear rounding costs must be integrated under the chosen threshold law.
teaching.followup: Why does choosing α uniformly all the way down to zero make this particular reciprocal expectation diverge?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: Retain a terminal with fractional retention mass y whenever y≥α. Let y=0.7 and α be uniform on [0.5,1]. With omission penalty 10, what is its expected penalty?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Worked example and its approximation accounting

teaching.summary: The terminal is omitted exactly when α>0.7. That event occupies length 0.3 in a support interval of length 0.5, so its probability is 0.6 and expected penalty is six. The endpoint equality convention has no effect for a continuous threshold distribution.
steps: Translate omission into the threshold event α>0.7.
Normalize its interval length: 0.3/0.5=0.6.
Multiply the omission probability by the penalty ten.
distractors: Correct: omission probability 0.6 times penalty ten is six.
Seven incorrectly uses the retention mass itself as omission probability.
Three uses an unnormalized interval length as a probability.
Four is the retained probability times penalty, the opposite event.
teaching.takeaway: The penalty analysis depends on the threshold distribution’s cumulative law.
teaching.followup: Replace the uniform threshold by a distribution with CDF F and express the expected penalty using F(0.7).

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: For retained terminals, the available tree rounding theorem costs at most twice the scaled fractional connection value. Scaling by 1/α makes their cuts feasible. At α=0.4, what coefficient multiplies the original connection LP cost?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: The threshold first changes the feasible connection solution by a factor 1/α. The tree rounding approximation then supplies an additional factor two, giving 2/α=5. A complete prize-collecting guarantee must also control omission penalties under the same threshold law; this question isolates only the connection part.
steps: Use retention to justify the reciprocal scaling of the fractional connection vector.
Apply the factor-two tree rounding theorem to that scaled vector.
Combine the factors to obtain 2/0.4=5.
distractors: Two and a half accounts for scaling but omits the tree rounding factor.
Correct: reciprocal scaling and factor two multiply to five.
Multiplication by α scales in the wrong direction for this feasibility repair.
Two ignores the threshold rescaling before rounding.
teaching.takeaway: Separate the two objective components before optimizing a shared random threshold.
teaching.followup: What happens to connection cost and omission penalties as α moves closer to one?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: A client’s fractional support is two facilities, each independently opened with probability 1/2. What is the probability neither support facility opens?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Worked example and its approximation accounting

teaching.summary: The two independent closure events each have probability one half, giving one quarter. Although the fractional assignments sum to one, this event can leave no opened supported facility for the client. Clustering and coordinated opening are introduced to guarantee service in every output, while controlling expected cost.
steps: Describe failure as both independent opening coins returning closed.
Distinguish expected fractional coverage from actual integral service.
distractors: Some outcomes do open a support facility, so failure is not certain.
A total fractional mass of one does not force an independent opening.
Correct: the unserved event has probability one quarter.
One half counts closure of only one specified support facility.
teaching.takeaway: An expected constraint is not the same as outcome-by-outcome feasibility.
teaching.followup: Give a coordinated opening rule on these two facilities that always opens exactly one.

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: A rerouting path from client j to an opened facility passes through two intermediate metric points, with segment lengths 2,3,4. What upper bound on direct connection distance follows from the metric inequality?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Worked example and its approximation accounting

teaching.summary: Repeated triangle inequality bounds the endpoint distance by the sum of the three segments, nine. It need not equal nine, because the direct route could be shorter. The facility-location proof must charge these segments to appropriate fractional or representative costs; a metric comparison alone does not finish the approximation ratio.
steps: Apply triangle inequality once to split off the first intermediate point.
Apply it again to bound the remaining two-segment route.
Add the three segment lengths to obtain nine.
distractors: Four keeps only the last segment and ignores the route to it.
Five accounts for only the first two segments.
Seven omits the first segment.
Correct: the full rerouting path bounds the direct distance by nine.
teaching.takeaway: Write the whole rerouting path before charging its edges.
teaching.followup: Which step would lack justification if the input connection costs were arbitrary nonmetric numbers?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: In the metric uncapacitated facility-location rounding proof, why may many clients be rerouted to one opened representative facility?
options: The facility has no service-capacity upper bound
All clients have zero connection cost
Each client’s original LP assignment was integral
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Limits and changed assumptions

teaching.summary: Uncapacitated means there is no limit on how many clients an opened facility serves. This allows the clustering repair to consolidate service without violating a capacity constraint, though connection distance and opening cost still have to be paid. A capacitated variant needs additional feasibility machinery; the same rerouting proof cannot simply be reused.
steps: Identify the feasibility condition changed by consolidating clients.
Use the absence of a service-capacity constraint to preserve feasibility.
Continue to charge every connection and the opening cost normally.
distractors: Correct: unrestricted service capacity permits consolidating clients.
The rerouted distances may be positive and require metric bounds.
Opening costs remain part of the objective and its expected analysis.
The algorithm begins from a fractional LP; integrality is not assumed.
teaching.takeaway: A rounding argument depends on the model’s feasibility constraints as well as its objective.
teaching.followup: Construct a unit-capacity facility example where this consolidation would fail.

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: A job has release date 5 and processing time 3. Its place in the rounded order is next, and the machine becomes free at time 2. What is its earliest legal nonpreemptive completion time?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Worked example and its approximation accounting

teaching.summary: The rounded order chooses which available position the job occupies, but release dates still restrict its start. Start at max(2,5)=5 and complete at eight. An ordering argument that starts it at time two would produce an infeasible schedule even if its weighted objective appeared better.
steps: Take the maximum of the machine’s free time and the release date.
Obtain legal start time five.
Add processing duration three to get completion eight.
distractors: Five is the legal start time rather than completion.
Correct: max(2,5)+3=8.
Three ignores both the current time and release date.
Ten adds an unnecessary additional wait of two.
teaching.takeaway: Rounding an order does not remove release-date feasibility.
teaching.followup: Why cannot a completion-time analysis silently replace max(machine-free time,release date) by machine-free time?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: A rounding analysis proves E[C₁]≤4 and E[C₂]≤10. With weights w₁=3 and w₂=2, what is the smallest upper bound supplied by these per-job estimates and linearity of expectation?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: The objective is 3C₁+2C₂, so linearity of expectation gives an upper bound 3·4+2·10=32. No independence of completion times is needed. Proving only an unweighted bound on C₁+C₂ would generally not justify this weighted conclusion, because the larger completion times might occur on more heavily weighted jobs.
steps: Write the actual objective with each job’s weight attached.
Apply linearity to get 3E[C₁]+2E[C₂].
Substitute the two per-job upper bounds to obtain 32.
distractors: Fourteen is the sum of the unweighted bounds.
Twenty-eight does not apply both stated weights correctly.
Correct: twelve plus twenty gives thirty-two.
Sixty does not follow from the two per-job bounds.
teaching.takeaway: Per-job expectation bounds transfer safely to nonnegative weighted objectives.
teaching.followup: Does this step require completion times of different jobs to be independent?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: A job’s normalized fractional processing reaches cumulative values 0.25,0.60,1 at time points 2,4,6. Defining its discrete α-point as the FIRST listed time with cumulative value at least α, which time is selected for α=0.5?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Worked example and its approximation accounting

teaching.summary: The first cumulative value meeting one half is 0.60 at time four. The α-point is defined through processed fraction, not by multiplying α by a final completion-time number. The question uses the stated discrete convention; a continuously processed interval would require its own interpolation convention.
steps: Compare α=0.5 against cumulative processing at time two; 0.25 is too small.
At time four, cumulative fraction 0.60 reaches the threshold.
Choose the first qualifying listed time, not a later point.
distractors: Five is not a listed time and no interpolation rule was specified.
Six reaches the threshold but is not the first such listed time.
At time two only one quarter of the processing has accumulated.
Correct: time four is the first listed threshold crossing.
teaching.takeaway: An α-point inverts cumulative processing; it is not automatically α times a completion time.
teaching.followup: How would the point change for α=0.8 under this same discrete convention?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: For an edge with unit-demand path-rounding load X, suppose a proved tail bound gives Pr[X≥a]≤0.001. There are 50 edges. What is the tightest simultaneous failure upper bound from the stated union-bound calculation, without assuming independent edge loads?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: The union bound adds the fifty bad-edge probabilities to obtain at most 0.05. Edge loads share sampled commodity paths and can be highly dependent, but the union bound requires no independence. Independence across commodities is used earlier when deriving a concentration bound for one edge.
steps: Define one bad event per edge.
Add their individual upper bounds: 50·0.001=0.05.
Conclude all capacities meet the chosen congestion threshold with probability at least 0.95.
distractors: Correct: the union bound gives failure at most five percent.
Multiplication would require a different event and independence assumptions not present here.
Ninety-five percent is the complementary lower bound on success, not failure.
One thousandth controls one edge, not all fifty.
teaching.takeaway: Keep the independence needed for a tail bound separate from the assumption-free union bound.
teaching.followup: If there are M edges and desired failure at most η, what per-edge bound is sufficient?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: Ten independent unit-demand commodities use an edge with probability 0.1 each. What is its expected load, and what does this expectation alone guarantee?
options: Mean 1, but larger realized loads remain possible
Mean 1 and deterministic load at most 1
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Worked example and its approximation accounting

teaching.summary: Linearity gives mean ten times one tenth, namely one. It does not rule out simultaneous choices by several commodities, including the positive-probability outcome in which all ten use the edge. A concentration argument is therefore needed to turn fractional or expected load control into a high-probability congestion statement.
steps: Represent edge load as the sum of ten path-use indicators.
Sum their expectations to obtain one.
Exhibit the all-use outcome as evidence that expectation is not a hard capacity bound.
distractors: One tenth is the probability for one commodity, not the total expectation.
Correct: expected load is one, with possible larger random congestion.
Ten is a possible maximum, not the expectation under these probabilities.
A mean of one does not bound every realization by one.
teaching.takeaway: Path sampling preserves each commodity’s route while only controlling edge loads probabilistically.
teaching.followup: What is the probability that all ten choose this edge under the stated independence?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: A path-rounding proof treats each commodity’s edge contribution as a Bernoulli variable. One commodity actually has demand 5. What must be repaired?
options: Nothing: an indicator times five is still bounded by one
The edge contribution’s magnitude must enter the MGF or normalization
The commodity must be split into unrelated endpoints
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Limits and changed assumptions

teaching.summary: The route-choice indicator is zero or one, but its contribution to load is zero or five. A unit-increment MGF bound cannot be used unchanged. Normalize by an appropriate demand bound or use a weighted-variable concentration estimate with explicit assumptions; path feasibility and the final union bound are separate matters.
steps: Distinguish the route-choice indicator from the amount of load it contributes.
Write the contribution as 5I rather than I.
Choose a weighted or normalized tail estimate before combining edge events.
distractors: The union bound remains valid; the faulty input is the per-edge tail calculation.
Multiplication by five changes the contribution’s range to zero or five.
Correct: load magnitudes determine the concentration parameters.
Changing endpoints does not repair the probabilistic estimate or preserve the commodity.
teaching.takeaway: A bounded-increment hypothesis must match the actual load units.
teaching.followup: For demand bound D, how would you rescale an edge load before applying a unit-range inequality?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: Sample each vertex independently with probability 1/2. For a vertex with three distinct neighbors, what is the probability none of its neighbors is sampled?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Worked example and its approximation accounting

teaching.summary: All three distinct neighbors must independently be omitted. Their omission probabilities multiply to one eighth. To dominate every vertex simultaneously, this single-vertex event must be controlled strongly enough to survive a union bound over all vertices; the calculation alone does not provide global domination.
steps: Identify the three neighbor-omission events.
Multiply their independent probabilities (1/2)^3.
Apply a separate union bound if the desired property concerns every vertex.
distractors: Three eighths counts a different binomial event, not no sampled neighbors.
One half is the omission probability for one neighbor.
The reciprocal degree is not the probability of three independent omissions.
Correct: three independent halves multiply to one eighth.
teaching.takeaway: A domination proof has a local sampling calculation and a global union bound.
teaching.followup: For sampling probability p and degree d, derive the exact miss probability and its exponential upper bound.

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: Suppose a sample has size exactly 2 log₃n. How many assignments of three colors to its vertices are enumerated?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: There are three choices per sampled vertex, hence 3 raised to the sample size. Substituting 2 log₃n gives n². More generally, O(log n/δ) sample size yields n to an exponent depending on 1/δ, which is polynomial in n for fixed density δ.
steps: Write the enumeration count as 3 to the power |S|.
Use 3^(log₃n)=n.
Square that identity because the sample size has the factor two.
distractors: Correct: 3^(2 log₃n)=n².
Two n replaces exponential enumeration by multiplication.
The logarithmic sample size does not multiply the input size in this count.
The extra leading three has no source in the specified exponent.
teaching.takeaway: Logarithmic sample size can permit exhaustive local guessing in polynomial time.
teaching.followup: What happens to this polynomial-time claim if δ is allowed to shrink with n?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: After coloring the sample, an edge uv has remaining lists L(u)={red,blue} and L(v)={blue,green}. Let U mean “u chooses blue” and V mean “v chooses blue.” Which 2SAT clause forbids this edge being monochromatic?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: The only shared color in the two lists is blue. The forbidden simultaneous choice is U and V both true, whose negation is ¬U∨¬V. A 2SAT instance adds such a clause for every same-color endpoint choice, preserving all proper extensions of the sampled coloring.
steps: Intersect the two lists to identify the only possible shared endpoint color.
Describe monochromaticity as U∧V.
Negate that bad assignment using De Morgan’s law.
distractors: U∨V requires at least one blue endpoint and still permits both blue.
Correct: the clause rules out exactly the simultaneous blue choice.
The conjunction U∧V enforces the forbidden assignment.
This forces neither endpoint blue and excludes valid extensions unnecessarily.
teaching.takeaway: Translate a forbidden local assignment into a clause rather than guessing its polarity.
teaching.followup: How many such clauses can one edge contribute when both endpoints have two allowed colors?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: Two unit vectors have angle π/3. Under random-hyperplane rounding, what are their separation probability and SDP edge contribution (1−cos θ)/2?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Worked example and its approximation accounting

teaching.summary: Angular separation gives probability θ/π=1/3. Since cos(π/3)=1/2, the relaxed edge contribution is (1−1/2)/2=1/4. They are different quantities; the approximation proof compares their ratio uniformly over all possible angles rather than identifying them.
steps: Use rotational symmetry to evaluate the cut probability as one third.
Evaluate the cosine-based relaxation term as one quarter.
Remember that a favorable ratio on this angle is not the worst-case algorithm factor.
distractors: The second entry uses the orthogonal-vector contribution, not this angle.
Neither stated quantity matches the two formulas at angle π/3.
Correct: hyperplane probability one third and SDP contribution one quarter.
This exchanges the probability and relaxation contribution.
teaching.takeaway: Compute the rounded event probability and relaxation value separately.
teaching.followup: Why can the edgewise ratio exceed one at this angle without proving a greater-than-one approximation factor?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: A matrix proposed as the Gram matrix of two unit vectors is [[1,2],[2,1]]. Why is it infeasible for the SDP?
options: Every feasible Gram matrix must have rank one
It has eigenvalue −1, so it is not positive semidefinite
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Worked example and its approximation accounting

teaching.summary: Unit diagonal is necessary but not sufficient. The vector (1,−1) has quadratic form −2 under this matrix, equivalently an eigenvalue −1, so the matrix is not PSD. Also, two unit vectors cannot have inner product two by Cauchy–Schwarz. The SDP relaxes the rank-one sign constraint but retains PSD feasibility.
steps: Check the diagonal; it passes the unit-norm test.
Evaluate X on the direction (1,−1), obtaining a negative quadratic form.
Reject PSD feasibility independently of any rounding procedure.
distractors: Removing the rank-one restriction is precisely part of the relaxation.
Both diagonal entries equal one, so this test actually passes.
Unit vectors can have nonzero inner product in feasible Gram matrices.
Correct: a negative eigenvalue violates the defining PSD constraint.
teaching.takeaway: A numerical or symbolic candidate must satisfy every relaxation constraint before its objective is meaningful.
teaching.followup: Repair the off-diagonal value to the largest feasible value and describe the corresponding two vectors.

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: An edgewise proof has pₑ≥αsₑ, then multiplies by edge weights and sums. What goes wrong if an edge weight is negative?
options: The negative weight reverses that edgewise inequality
The hyperplane is no longer random
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Limits and changed assumptions

teaching.summary: The angular probability calculation and Gram representation still make sense. The failure is in turning a lower probability comparison into a lower weighted-objective comparison: multiplying by a negative coefficient reverses the inequality. Therefore the standard summation proof requires nonnegative edge weights or a separate treatment of negative ones.
steps: Identify exactly which line multiplies the probability comparison by wₑ.
Use elementary order rules when wₑ<0.
Keep the nonnegative-weight hypothesis attached to the approximation theorem.
distractors: Correct: the edgewise lower bound no longer gives the needed weighted lower bound.
Changing an objective weight does not stop the chosen hyperplane from being random.
The same unit-vector Gram representation can remain well defined.
Order reverses when multiplying an inequality by a negative number.
teaching.takeaway: Check sign hypotheses before summing local approximation inequalities.
teaching.followup: Give numerical p,s,α,w with p≥αs but wp≤wαs when w<0.

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: An edge’s vector angle is at least 2π/3. With three independent random hyperplanes, what is the maximum probability its endpoints get the same three-bit sign label?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Worked example and its approximation accounting

teaching.summary: One hyperplane fails to separate the endpoints with probability at most 1/3. Matching all three sign bits requires three such failures, and the hyperplanes are independent, so the probability is at most (1/3)^3. The labels use at most 2³=8 colors, but the count of labels is not the edge-collision probability.
steps: Use the angle lower bound to obtain separation probability at least two thirds.
Complement to get same-sign probability at most one third per plane.
Multiply the independent per-plane collision bounds for the three-bit labels.
distractors: One ninth uses only two independent planes.
Correct: three independent collisions cost at most one twenty-seventh.
One eighth is the reciprocal number of labels, not this geometry-based collision bound.
One third is the bound for only one hyperplane.
teaching.takeaway: The rounding distribution is not a uniform independent color choice per vertex.
teaching.followup: How many hyperplanes make the expected number of monochromatic edges at most n/8 in a graph with maximum degree Δ?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: Let a=log₃2. Balancing the color bounds n/σ and σᵃ requires which choice of σ?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: Set n/σ=σᵃ and multiply by σ to obtain n=σ^(1+a). Thus σ=n^(1/(1+a)), and the balanced color exponent is a/(1+a)=log₆2≈0.38685. The exponent comes from balancing two algorithmic regimes, not from simply quoting the one-plane separation probability.
steps: Equate the two competing upper bounds.
Solve σ^(1+a)=n for the threshold.
Substitute back to identify the shared cost n^(a/(1+a)).
distractors: Subtracting exponents does not solve this product equation.
A fixed fraction of n does not balance n/σ with a positive power of σ.
Correct: this choice equalizes the high-degree and low-degree costs.
Choosing n^a generally leaves the two terms with different exponents.
teaching.takeaway: Derive balancing exponents from an equation and verify by substitution.
teaching.followup: What extra factor appears when a constant-fraction semicoloring is repeated to color all vertices?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: A semicoloring step properly colors a constant fraction of remaining vertices. Why use fresh color palettes on different recursive rounds?
options: The SDP requires all color names to be different
The previously colored subgraph stops being proper
Edges between rounds might connect vertices given the same reused color
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Limits and changed assumptions

teaching.summary: Properness within each selected subset does not control edges joining subsets colored in different rounds. Reusing a palette can make such an edge monochromatic. Fresh palettes prevent cross-round conflicts, while the geometric decrease in remaining vertices requires O(log n) rounds and accounts for the logarithmic overhead.
steps: Distinguish edges internal to one round from edges between rounds.
Note that the semicoloring guarantee addresses the former only.
Assign disjoint palettes to make cross-round endpoint colors automatically different.
distractors: The rounding step does not make all graph edges disappear.
The palette rule is an integral coloring repair, not a PSD matrix constraint.
An already proper induced coloring remains proper internally.
Correct: the missing constraint concerns edges between separately colored subsets.
teaching.takeaway: A partial-solution guarantee must be composed with a proof controlling interactions between pieces.
teaching.followup: How would you bound the total color count if each round uses at most K colors and removes at least half the remaining vertices?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: Adjacent unit vectors have Gaussian projections Z₁,Z₂ with correlation −1/2. What is Var(Z₁+Z₂)?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Worked example and its approximation accounting

teaching.summary: Each projection has variance one. The sum variance is 1+1+2(−1/2)=1. Consequently, simultaneous exceedance of a positive threshold t implies a sum exceeding 2t with this small variance, giving a useful joint-tail estimate; treating the projections as independent would lose the negative correlation.
steps: Write variance of a sum with the covariance term included.
Use covariance equal to correlation because both variances are one.
Compute 2−1=1 and apply the sum-tail comparison if needed.
distractors: Correct: the negative covariance lowers sum variance to one.
Two drops the covariance and treats the projections as uncorrelated.
Three has the wrong sign for the covariance contribution.
Perfect cancellation would require correlation minus one, not minus one half.
teaching.takeaway: The edge constraint helps through a joint Gaussian tail, not merely marginal survival probabilities.
teaching.followup: Why does Z₁≥t and Z₂≥t imply an event for Z₁+Z₂ that is easier to bound?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: A Gaussian selection has expected retained vertices 20 and expected retained edges 6. Deleting at most one endpoint per surviving edge guarantees what expected independent-set size?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Worked example and its approximation accounting

teaching.summary: For every selected graph S, processing surviving edges and deleting one endpoint when needed leaves an independent set of size at least |S|−e(S). Taking expectations gives at least twenty minus six, fourteen, without requiring independence between the vertex and edge counts. The bound can be loose if one deletion removes many edges.
steps: Prove the pointwise repair inequality before averaging.
Use linearity of expectation on |S|−e(S).
Substitute the two expectations to obtain a lower bound of fourteen.
distractors: Six counts expected retained edges, not a maximum independent-set size.
Correct: alteration yields an expected lower bound of fourteen.
A lower bound need not be exact because repair can remove fewer than six vertices.
The retained set can contain edges, so not all twenty expected vertices are guaranteed to survive.
teaching.takeaway: Alteration arguments combine dependent quantities through a pointwise inequality and linearity.
teaching.followup: Explain why the same lower bound remains valid when all selections use one shared Gaussian direction.

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: Why is it generally wrong to replace the adjacent-pair selection probability in Gaussian-vector rounding by q², where q is one vertex’s selection probability?
options: All vertices have different marginal laws
The common Gaussian direction correlates the two projection events
Every adjacent pair is selected with probability one
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Limits and changed assumptions

teaching.summary: All unit-vector projections can have the same standard normal marginal while their joint laws depend on vector inner products. A common Gaussian direction makes neighboring selection events correlated, and the negative edge correlation is precisely what suppresses joint survival. The product q² would require independence, not equal marginals.
steps: Identify the common random Gaussian vector used for both endpoints.
Compute their projection covariance from the two unit vectors’ inner product.
Use the joint Gaussian law or a sum-tail argument, rather than multiplying marginals.
distractors: The marginal is well defined; the difficulty is the joint event.
Unit-vector projections have the same standard normal marginal in this construction.
Correct: shared randomness and nonzero inner product create dependence.
A positive threshold does not force every adjacent pair to survive.
teaching.takeaway: Equal marginal distributions do not imply independent events.
teaching.followup: What inner-product condition makes two Gaussian projections independent, and why is it different from the promised negative edge correlation?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: A primal–dual set-cover solution costs 36 and a feasible dual has value 12. If each element is charged at most f=3 times through selected tight sets, what is the strongest ratio certified by this frequency accounting?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: Selected tight sets have costs equal to sums of the element duals they contain. Summing their costs charges any element at most f times, so cost≤3·12=36. Weak duality gives dual value≤OPT, completing the 3-approximation comparison; equality with this dual does not show the primal is optimal.
steps: Replace each selected tight set’s cost by its sum of contained dual variables.
Bound each element’s multiplicity by three.
Use weak duality to compare twelve with the integral optimum.
distractors: Twelve is the dual objective value, not a dimensionless approximation factor.
The solution cost can be three times the exhibited lower bound, so optimality is not certified.
The stated frequency bound is three, not two.
Correct: tightness, bounded frequency, and weak duality certify factor three.
teaching.takeaway: An approximation factor is the maximum charging multiplicity, not the dual value itself.
teaching.followup: Which assumption would you need to improve the same argument from factor three to factor two?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: For the standard frequency bound in primal–dual set cover, f is which quantity?
options: The largest number of sets containing one element
The largest cardinality of one set
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: The proof groups selected tight-set costs by element dual variables. An element’s dual can be charged once for each selected set containing that element, so the relevant worst-case parameter is its incidence frequency. Maximum set cardinality instead bounds a different direction of the incidence relation and is not the parameter in this charging step.
steps: Write the cost sum over selected tight sets.
Exchange summations so each element dual carries a multiplicity.
Bound that multiplicity by the number of available sets containing the element.
distractors: Correct: element incidence frequency limits how often the same dual mass is counted.
Set cardinality counts elements per set, the opposite direction of incidence.
Total universe size gives only a crude different parameter, not the stated frequency.
Minimum cost does not bound how many selected sets charge an element.
teaching.takeaway: Read a charging factor from the index that survives after exchanging sums.
teaching.followup: Build a system with one huge set but every element in only two sets, and identify its f bound.

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: A set is selected before it is tight, and the proof writes its cost as the sum of its element dual values. What is missing?
options: An equality justified by tightness or a replacement cost bound
A proof that all dual variables are one
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Limits and changed assumptions

teaching.summary: Dual feasibility provides sum of contained duals≤set cost, a lower bound on that cost. The approximation analysis needs an upper bound on selected cost in terms of dual mass. Tightness supplies equality; selecting a slack set removes that justification unless a separate bounded-slack argument is established.
steps: State the dual constraint in its correct direction.
Notice that feasibility alone cannot upper-bound a selected set’s cost by contained dual mass.
Require tightness or prove the exact replacement inequality the charging step needs.
distractors: The broken step is an objective comparison even if the algorithm is fast.
Correct: a slack constraint supplies the wrong inequality direction for that substitution.
Randomness does not repair the missing cost equality.
Dual variables need not equal one or be integral.
teaching.takeaway: A lower-bound certificate does not automatically pay for arbitrary primal choices.
teaching.followup: Can approximate tightness with cost≤c times contained dual mass yield a modified approximation factor?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: A selected s–t subgraph is the triangle with edge costs 1,1,2, where the two unit edges form an s–t path. Removing the cost-2 edge preserves connectivity. What does this illustrate about a growth-based algorithm’s cost proof?
options: All selected edges must remain forever
Cleanup can remove redundant paid edges before charging the final path
Reverse deletion always makes every graph bipartite
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: The selected subgraph is feasible both before and after removing the direct edge, but its cost drops from four to two. A shortest-path primal–dual analysis must therefore charge the cleaned final path rather than indiscriminately count every edge that became selected. This example illustrates redundancy, not a claim about which edges a particular growth schedule selects.
steps: Check that the two unit edges already connect s to t.
Compare selected-subgraph costs before and after deleting the redundant direct edge.
Distinguish the algorithm’s growth history from the object used in its final charging proof.
distractors: Redundant edges can be removed while keeping the required path.
Feasible subgraphs can have widely different costs.
Correct: pruning changes what cost must be justified by the dual.
The point is preserving one path, not a general bipartiteness algorithm.
teaching.takeaway: Prove the guarantee for the final cleaned solution, not just the collection of growth events.
teaching.followup: Why can an inclusion-minimal connected s–t subgraph with nonnegative edge costs be taken to be a simple path?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: A shortest-path dual certificate has value 7, and a feasible final path of cost 7 is constructed. What follows by weak duality?
options: The graph has exactly seven edges
OPT=7 and the path is optimal
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Worked example and its approximation accounting

teaching.summary: A feasible path gives OPT≤7 for this minimization problem. A feasible dual of value seven gives 7≤OPT. The matching upper and lower bounds force equality. Unlike many approximation proofs, this case closes without a multiplicative loss, but only because both feasibility statements and the equality of objectives are established.
steps: Use primal feasibility to upper-bound the optimum by the path cost.
Use dual feasibility to lower-bound the optimum by the certificate value.
Combine 7≤OPT≤7.
distractors: All stated costs support a positive optimum, not a nonpositive one.
A factor-two statement is weaker than the exact equality proved here.
Cost seven does not determine the number of graph edges.
Correct: matching feasible primal and dual values certify exact optimality.
teaching.takeaway: Matching primal and dual certificates prove equality only when both certificates are valid.
teaching.followup: If the path cost were ten and dual value seven, which approximation ratio would this pair certify?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: A proof counts all edges selected during dual growth, although reverse deletion later removes some. Why is that potentially the wrong object to analyze?
options: The charging identity may rely on how the FINAL path crosses positive dual cuts
Every connected graph is already a path
Deleted edges still contribute to the returned path’s cost
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Limits and changed assumptions

teaching.summary: The final charging identity counts, for each dual cut, how many returned path edges cross it. Earlier selected edges can create redundancy or extra crossings that do not belong to the final path. Reverse deletion is therefore part of the mathematical structure supporting the cost comparison, not merely an optional implementation optimization.
steps: Express the final path cost using its edge set.
Exchange the edge and cut sums after using the appropriate tightness identities.
Verify the crossing property for the pruned path rather than assuming it for all selected edges.
distractors: Correct: cleanup can be essential to the cut-crossing multiplicity needed in the proof.
Dual feasibility still supplies the lower bound throughout the argument.
A connected subgraph may contain branches and cycles.
Returned cost counts retained edges; removed ones do not contribute.
teaching.takeaway: When pruning appears in an algorithm, locate the exact proof property it establishes.
teaching.followup: How would a positive dual cut crossed repeatedly by the retained solution alter its cost accounting?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: In a Steiner-forest moat-growth proof, an active contracted component has degree five in the pruned forest. Does that alone contradict the factor-two charging argument?
options: Yes; forests have maximum degree two
No; the proof bounds an aggregate degree sum, not each component separately
Yes; every active component has degree at most two
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Limits and changed assumptions

teaching.summary: A forest can have a high-degree center, so degree five is not itself a contradiction. The moat-growth analysis controls the sum of crossings over active components using a global forest argument and properties of inactive components after pruning. Replacing that aggregate statement by an individual degree bound would make the proof false.
steps: Recall that a star is a forest with arbitrarily large center degree.
Identify the proof’s sum over active components during one growth interval.
Use the pruning and inactivity conditions in the aggregate bound.
distractors: Forests are acyclic but need not have maximum degree two.
Correct: aggregate forest charging permits some components to have larger degree.
Degrees are central to the aggregate crossing calculation.
An individual degree-two claim is false for branching demand structures.
teaching.takeaway: Do not strengthen a summed combinatorial inequality into an unsupported pointwise one.
teaching.followup: Draw a star with five leaves and explain which degree statement survives for the whole tree.

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: Three active components each grow their dual at unit rate for time Δ=2. If the pruned-forest crossing lemma charges at most twice total dual growth, what is the smallest cost-charge upper bound supplied by the factor-two lemma for this interval?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: The dual objective grows by three active components times two time units, namely six. The aggregate forest lemma allows cost charge at most twice that increase, hence twelve. This local interval accounting is integrated over the entire growth process and then compared with OPT using dual feasibility.
steps: Count active dual variables growing in the interval.
Multiply count three by duration two to obtain dual increase six.
Apply the factor-two aggregate crossing bound to obtain twelve.
distractors: Three omits the interval duration.
Six is the dual increase before the crossing factor two.
Correct: at most twice the dual increase six is twelve.
Eighteen introduces an additional factor of three without justification.
teaching.takeaway: A growth-interval proof must account for rate, duration, and crossing multiplicity separately.
teaching.followup: How do you combine consecutive intervals when the number of active components changes?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: Which condition makes a component active in the generalized Steiner-forest growth algorithm?
options: It has the largest number of vertices
It contains any terminal at all
It separates at least one required pair that is still disconnected
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: Activity is defined by unmet connectivity requirements. A component can contain terminals yet be inactive if every required mate is already connected within it. Conversely, it becomes relevant to growth when a required pair is separated by its boundary. This definition is needed to justify both dual constraints and pruning behavior.
steps: Inspect the specified list of demand pairs, rather than just a set of terminal vertices.
Ask whether a component boundary separates a pair whose endpoints must be joined.
Grow the dual only for components active under that separation requirement.
distractors: Component size does not determine which demands remain unsatisfied.
Containing a terminal does not imply any unsatisfied demand crosses the boundary.
Degree parity does not define activity in this algorithm.
Correct: an unfulfilled separated demand pair makes its component active.
teaching.takeaway: A primal–dual active set is determined by the problem’s actual demand constraints.
teaching.followup: Give a component containing two terminals that is nevertheless inactive.

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: Take a six-cycle with unit edge lengths. Delete one edge to form an MST path. For the endpoints of the deleted edge, what is tree distance divided by original graph distance?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Worked example and its approximation accounting

teaching.summary: The original endpoints are adjacent, so their graph distance is one. In the MST path the only connecting route traverses the other five edges, giving stretch five. Extending the example to an n-cycle yields stretch n−1 for that pair and shows why simply choosing an MST is not the required expected logarithmic-distortion construction.
steps: Identify the pair whose direct edge was deleted.
Compute the unique tree route length as five.
Divide by its original shortest-path distance one.
distractors: Correct: the pair’s distance increases from one to five.
Six counts the whole original cycle rather than its five-edge tree path.
The deleted pair no longer has its direct unit route in the tree.
Two does not account for the full remaining path around the cycle.
teaching.takeaway: A good spanning-tree cost does not imply small distortion for every pair.
teaching.followup: How does this example scale with n, and which expected-stretch claim does random embedding replace it with?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: A fixed benchmark uses two graph edges with distances 1 and 2 and cost coefficients 3 and 4. Each pair’s expected tree distance is at most three times its original distance. What is the strongest numerical upper bound on expected benchmark tree cost supplied by the stated factor-three expectation estimate?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: The original weighted cost is 3·1+4·2=11. Linearity lets the pairwise expected-stretch bound act on each fixed coefficient, giving expected tree cost at most 3·11=33. Distances of different pairs need not be independent, but the benchmark being charged must be fixed before the tree is sampled.
steps: Compute the original benchmark’s weighted length eleven.
Apply the factor-three expectation bound to each edge’s pair distance.
Sum the two terms by linearity to obtain thirty-three.
distractors: Twenty-two applies stretch two instead of the stated three.
Correct: expected cost is at most three times eleven.
Forty-four has no support in the stated stretch factor.
Eleven is the original benchmark value before applying stretch.
teaching.takeaway: Pairwise expectation bounds sum for a fixed nonnegative weighted benchmark without independence.
teaching.followup: Why cannot the same line automatically replace a fixed benchmark by a maximum chosen after seeing the sampled tree?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: For concave nondecreasing capacity cost f(x)=√x with f(0)=0, two routed capacities 9 and 16 merge on one graph edge. Which comparison supports the buy-at-bulk transfer?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Limits and changed assumptions

teaching.summary: Merging the capacities costs √25=5, no more than the separate charges √9+√16=7. The transfer proof uses this subadditivity to ensure that overlap of tree-edge routes does not make a graph edge cost exceed the sum already charged to those routes. Concavity with f(0)=0 supplies the needed general inequality.
steps: Add capacities before evaluating the shared-edge cost.
Compute √25=5 and the separate total 3+4=7.
Use the subadditive direction to compare merged cost with previously charged costs.
distractors: Seven is the separate-cost total, not the merged cost.
The inequality direction would obstruct rather than support this transfer.
Correct: merged capacity benefits from the concave cost.
The cost is the square root, not the identity function.
teaching.takeaway: State the capacity-cost assumption that makes shared routing affordable.
teaching.followup: Show why a convex cost f(x)=x² would reverse the useful behavior on this example.

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: An optimum independent set has 35 vertices. With k=7 layer residues, what is the strongest retained-size lower bound given by the one-seventh averaging argument?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Worked example and its approximation accounting

teaching.summary: Each optimum vertex belongs to exactly one residue class, so the seven loss counts sum to 35. One deletion therefore loses at most five optimum vertices, leaving at least thirty. The algorithm need not know the optimum: it solves the residual problems for every residue and keeps the best result.
steps: Partition the unknown optimum by layer residue modulo seven.
Apply averaging to find a residue with loss at most 35/7=5.
Subtract that loss and rely on exact residual optimization for the candidate guarantee.
distractors: Some optimum vertices may be deleted; all thirty-five are not guaranteed to survive.
Five bounds a favorable loss, not the retained optimum size.
Twenty-eight is a weaker number that does not use the stated one-seventh loss accurately.
Correct: at least six sevenths of thirty-five is thirty.
teaching.takeaway: Average over the unknown optimum, then enumerate choices so the algorithm finds a candidate at least as good.
teaching.followup: Why does the averaging argument still hold for nonnegative vertex weights?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: At a join bag in independent-set DP, two child values for the same chosen bag set S are 9 and 11, and |S|=3. If both child values include S, what is the joined value?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: Both child subproblems contain the shared bag. Adding their values counts the three selected bag vertices twice, while all other counted vertices lie in disjoint child regions. Subtract the common bag contribution once, giving 9+11−3=17. The state must also enforce that S is independent.
steps: Check the counting convention: both children include the bag.
Add the two child values, giving twenty.
Remove one duplicate count of the three bag vertices.
distractors: Correct: the join recurrence gives seventeen.
Fourteen subtracts the shared bag twice rather than once.
Twenty double-counts every selected vertex in the shared bag.
Twenty-three adds the duplicate bag contribution instead of subtracting it.
teaching.takeaway: Write what a DP value counts before deriving a join recurrence.
teaching.followup: What term replaces |S| in a vertex-weighted independent-set DP?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: The planar-layer argument deletes one residue and obtains treewidth O(k). Why does this not establish the same PTAS on arbitrary graphs?
options: Independent sets have no optimum outside planar graphs
The structural treewidth bound uses planarity or bounded outerplanarity
Dynamic programming can never solve nonplanar graphs
Averaging over residues is false outside planar graphs
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Limits and changed assumptions

teaching.summary: The averaging step is a counting fact and does not require planarity. The crucial source-specific input is that deleting one residue of the assigned planar outer-face layers leaves components of bounded outerplanarity and hence bounded treewidth. Without the structural theorem the residual instances may remain hard despite a small loss from the optimum.
steps: Separate the universal averaging fact from the graph-structure claim.
Identify where the bounded-outerplanarity theorem bounds treewidth by O(k).
Recognize that exact bounded-width DP is useful only after this width guarantee is established.
distractors: Every finite graph has a maximum independent set.
Correct: the residual-width theorem is the model-dependent ingredient.
Bounded-treewidth dynamic programming also applies to nonplanar inputs when a decomposition is supplied.
Partition averaging holds for any finite optimum set.
teaching.takeaway: A structural approximation method needs both a small deletion loss and tractable residual structure.
teaching.followup: Would an arbitrary vertex partition into k classes supply the same width guarantee even on a planar graph?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: A MAX gap reduction yields YES OPT≥0.9M and NO OPT≤0.63M. Under the convention ALG≥ρOPT, what strict condition guarantees separation by the output value?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Worked example and its approximation accounting

teaching.summary: A YES output is at least 0.9ρM, whereas every feasible NO output is at most 0.63M. Strictly separating these ranges requires 0.9ρ>0.63, or ρ>0.7. Equality does not ensure a distinguishable threshold, so preserving strict inequalities matters in an inapproximability proof.
steps: Write the guaranteed YES output lower bound in the stated ratio convention.
Use feasibility to retain the NO optimum as an upper bound on every output.
Solve 0.9ρ>0.63.
distractors: Small positive guarantees can fall entirely inside the NO range.
The inequality is reversed; a weaker lower guarantee cannot force separation.
Correct: the ratio must beat the NO-to-YES threshold 0.7.
Choosing the NO fraction itself does not compare it with the YES completeness value.
teaching.takeaway: Always derive the gap threshold in the ratio convention actually being used.
teaching.followup: How would you rewrite the condition under the convention ALG≥OPT/α with α≥1?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: A PCP verifier uses r=3 log₂n random bits and five queries. How many local tests are created when a gap-CSP reduction enumerates its random tapes?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: There is one test for each random tape, hence 2ʳ=n³ tests. Five queries keep each constraint’s arity constant, but do not reduce the number of random tapes to five. The reduction must impose all these tests on a single global assignment to proof positions to preserve soundness.
steps: Count binary random tapes as two raised to the random-bit count.
Substitute r=3 log₂n and simplify to n³.
Keep constant query arity separate from the polynomial number of tests.
distractors: This would correspond to a linear rather than logarithmic number of random bits.
Three n treats a logarithmic random-bit count as a multiplier.
Five controls queries per test, not the number of tests.
Correct: enumerating random tapes creates polynomially many, namely n cubed, tests.
teaching.takeaway: Randomness controls test count; query complexity controls local constraint arity.
teaching.followup: Why would giving every test its own independent proof assignment destroy the gap reduction?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: A parity-to-3SAT gadget gives four satisfied clauses for a satisfied parity constraint and three for an unsatisfied one. If at most half the parity constraints can be satisfied, what is the strongest clause-satisfaction fraction upper bound supplied by this gadget calculation?
questions.skill: Identify and justify the decisive approximation step
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: The average gadget contributes at most half of four plus half of three, or 3.5 satisfied clauses out of four. The resulting fraction is 3.5/4=7/8. A complete hardness statement retains small completeness and soundness errors and proves that one global truth assignment induces these gadget values consistently.
steps: Group parity constraints into satisfied and unsatisfied classes under a fixed assignment.
Use the at-most-half hypothesis and the gadget’s two payoff values.
Normalize the maximum average 3.5 by four clauses per gadget.
distractors: Correct: averaging gadget payoffs gives seven eighths.
A positive fraction of parity violations prevents all gadget clauses being satisfied.
One half is the parity satisfaction fraction, before the gadget baseline is added.
Three quarters counts only the unsatisfied gadget value and ignores satisfied constraints.
teaching.takeaway: A gadget’s baseline payoff shifts a gap; compute the new ratio rather than copying the source fraction.
teaching.followup: How does the calculation change if the parity soundness fraction is 1/2+η?

questions.subject: approx

questions.question: For A with rows (1,1,0), (0,1,1), (1,0,1), how many perfect matchings does its permanent count?
questions.skill: Expand a permanent as a count
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Expand a permanent as a count

teaching.summary: A permanent chooses one entry in every row and every column, then sums the products without signs. Here only two permutations use exclusively 1-entries. This connects the counting problem that LFKN verifies to a concrete combinatorial object.
steps: If row 1 uses column 1, row 3 must use column 3 and row 2 column 2: one matching.
If row 1 uses column 2, row 2 must use column 3 and row 3 column 1: one more matching.
Row 1 cannot use column 3 because its entry is zero. These cases exhaust its choices.
distractors: Correct: the identity permutation and the cyclic column choice (2,3,1) each contribute 1.
The three rows are not three independent choices; each selected column must be used once.
There are six permutations, but four products contain a zero and contribute nothing.
There are two valid choices for the first row, and each extends to a distinct matching.
teaching.takeaway: A 0–1 permanent counts feasible permutations; it does not count all permutations.
teaching.followup: Replace the lower-left 1 by 0 and recalculate the permanent. Which matching disappears?

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: A proposed sum-check verifier reveals the random evaluation point before the prover commits to its round polynomial. Which soundness argument is now missing?
options: The polynomial root bound is false over finite fields.
The dishonest difference polynomial is fixed independently of the fresh evaluation point.
The honest prover must know all future random coins.
The verifier must enumerate every Boolean assignment.
questions.skill: Respect the message–randomness order
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Respect the message–randomness order

teaching.summary: The root bound concerns one fixed nonzero polynomial evaluated at a fresh uniform point. If the prover can choose the polynomial after seeing that point, it can arrange a root there. Algebraic degree control alone therefore does not supply the usual probability bound.
steps: Condition on the transcript before the next random challenge; the alleged polynomial must already be fixed.
Compare that fixed message with the honest polynomial. A nonzero difference has at most its degree many roots.
Sampling only afterward turns the root count into a probability. Adaptive choice after sampling breaks this implication.
distractors: The root bound remains valid; the problem is applying it to a polynomial chosen from the sampled point.
Correct: the argument needs a fixed difference polynomial before the fresh randomness is exposed.
The honest prover computes its current restriction from the past, not from future coins.
The protocol avoids exponential enumeration by evaluating its final polynomial claim directly.
teaching.takeaway: In interactive soundness, who commits before which random choice is part of the theorem.
teaching.followup: Give a family of nonzero linear polynomials chosen after r is revealed, each vanishing at that r.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: A valid sum-check uses four rounds, individual degree at most 3, and fresh uniform challenges in F₁₀₁. What is the numerical value of the standard first-false-claim union-bound expression?
questions.skill: Accumulate conditional root errors
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Accumulate conditional root errors

teaching.summary: Each round can turn an incorrect claim into a correct one only at a root of a nonzero polynomial of degree at most 3. Condition on the past and add the four round-error bounds. No independence between cheating messages is required.
steps: For any fixed preceding transcript with a false claim, the next accidental agreement has probability at most 3/101.
If an initially false claim reaches an accepted direct final evaluation, some round must have repaired the false claim.
The union bound over four possible repair rounds gives 4·3/101=12/101.
distractors: This controls only one round and omits the other chances for accidental agreement.
This counts rounds but drops the degree-three factor in each root bound.
Correct: multiply the number of rounds by the individual-degree bound, then divide by field size.
This has no field-size denominator and is not the probability estimate supplied by the proof.
teaching.takeaway: Soundness accounting tracks both the number of opportunities to cheat and each opportunity’s degree.
teaching.followup: If different rounds have degree bounds 1,2,3,4, derive the analogous field-size bound.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: Five adaptively selected counting claims are verified, with conditional soundness error at most 0.002 per claim. What is the tightest overall bound supplied by adding these five estimates, without assuming independence?
questions.skill: Budget errors for adaptive oracle claims
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Budget errors for adaptive oracle claims

teaching.summary: Adaptivity does not prevent a union bound. The guarantee must hold conditional on each legal earlier transcript. A false computation accepted through five checked claims must include a false accepted answer, and that event has probability at most the sum of the five bounds.
steps: Fix the past before each checked claim; the local soundness guarantee remains at most 0.002.
Name the bad event that this check accepts an incorrect counting answer.
The probability that any of the five bad events occurs is at most 5·0.002=0.01.
distractors: A product would require a different event and additional conditions; one bad accepted claim may suffice.
This omits four possible incorrect answers and is only a per-check bound.
This is the complement of the upper bound, a lower bound on avoiding all bad events.
Correct: a union bound adds the five error budgets even when the claims depend on earlier answers.
teaching.takeaway: A class-level consequence requires error and resource budgets for the whole adaptive computation.
teaching.followup: Choose a per-claim error budget for q claims if the desired total error is at most η.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: A verifier establishes that a nonnegative integer permanent is 3 modulo 7. The known upper bound is 20. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The integer permanent is one of 3, 10, or 17.
questions.skill: Separate a residue claim from an integer claim
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Separate a residue claim from an integer claim

teaching.summary: A correct field computation determines a residue, not automatically an integer. The interval bound restricts possible representatives. Exact counting verification needs sufficient modulus size or justified reconstruction from several residues.
steps: List nonnegative numbers congruent to 3 modulo 7: 3,10,17,24 and so on.
Intersect this list with the promised interval from 0 to 20, leaving three possibilities.
A modulus exceeding the entire possible range would identify the integer uniquely; 7 does not.
distractors: Correct: all three listed numbers satisfy both the residue and the interval promise.
The residual ambiguity is deterministic; a root-bound error cannot turn it into exact identification.
This selects the smallest representative but has not ruled out 10 or 17.
Congruence to 3 modulo 7 places no primality constraint on the integer.
teaching.takeaway: Always specify whether a claimed counting value lives in a field or in the integers.
teaching.followup: What smallest strict inequality on a single modulus would ensure uniqueness for every count in [0,20]?

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: Suppose the required reductions establish PH⊆P^#P and a separately proved protocol simulation establishes P^#P⊆IP. What follows by composition alone?
questions.skill: Distinguish containment from hierarchy collapse
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Distinguish containment from hierarchy collapse

teaching.summary: Containments compose in their stated direction. A protocol for the counting-oracle computation places PH inside IP, but does not identify IP with a fixed hierarchy level or prove that the hierarchy collapses.
steps: Begin with an arbitrary language in PH and apply the first containment to obtain a counting-oracle computation.
Apply the second assumed containment to that computation, preserving its language.
Conclude membership in IP. No reverse containment or fixed-level simulation was among the assumptions.
distractors: This reverses the derived containment and is not supplied by either premise.
Correct: transitivity yields PH⊆IP and nothing stronger by itself.
A collapse to level two requires an additional hypothesis or theorem identifying such a level.
Equality with NP would need a further reduction of all hierarchy levels to NP.
teaching.takeaway: State the exact conclusion of a containment chain before discussing stronger consequences.
teaching.followup: What additional containment involving IP would be sufficient to infer PH=NP from these premises?

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: Over F₁₀₁ let f(X,Y)=X²Y+XY². Apply Boolean multilinearization first in X and then in Y. What polynomial results, and what is its value at (2,3)?
questions.skill: Compute a degree-reduction operator
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Compute a degree-reduction operator

teaching.summary: Boolean multilinearization replaces each variable’s dependence by interpolation between its values at 0 and 1. It preserves the Boolean table, rather than every field evaluation. Applying it twice makes the distinction visible.
steps: In X, f(0,Y)=0 and f(1,Y)=Y+Y², so Rₓf=XY+XY².
In Y, this polynomial is zero at Y=0 and 2X at Y=1, giving RᵧRₓf=2XY.
The reduced value at (2,3) is 12, whereas the original gives 30. Both agree on Boolean inputs.
distractors: This is the result after the first reduction only; Y still has degree two.
This drops one of the two monomials’ contributions at the Boolean point (1,1).
Correct: reducing both variables sends both original monomials to XY, giving 2XY.
The reduction preserves Boolean values, not the entire original polynomial over the field.
teaching.takeaway: A protocol must verify degree reduction as a transformation, not assume all evaluations are preserved.
teaching.followup: Check equality of the original and reduced polynomials at all four Boolean points.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: Using the Boolean existential-quantifier polynomial 1−(1−f|y=0)(1−f|y=1), eliminate y from f(x,y)=xy. What polynomial remains?
questions.skill: Arithmetize an existential quantifier
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Arithmetize an existential quantifier

teaching.summary: Existential quantification acts as Boolean OR over the two restrictions. For xy those restrictions are 0 and x, so the OR polynomial is x. This calculation checks the operator before considering its degree growth in a large formula.
steps: Set y=0 to obtain f₀(x)=0, and set y=1 to obtain f₁(x)=x.
Substitute in the existential operator: 1−(1−0)(1−x).
Simplify to x. On Boolean inputs, a suitable y makes xy true exactly when x=1.
distractors: Multiplying restrictions is the universal operator, and here that product would be zero.
This is the universal result for the two restrictions, not their existential result.
Simply adding the variable twice does not implement OR and can fail already at x=1.
Correct: the existential operator is OR of the two restrictions, yielding x.
teaching.takeaway: Translate a quantifier into its operator and evaluate its two restrictions explicitly.
teaching.followup: Now eliminate y universally from xy and explain why the result changes.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: A correctly scheduled arithmetization has 12 operator checks, each with degree at most 4. Which listed prime field size makes the union-bound soundness estimate at most 0.1?
questions.skill: Choose a field from the complete error budget
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Choose a field from the complete error budget

teaching.summary: The relevant budget is the sum of every operator’s degree bound. A field adequate for one check can be inadequate for the entire protocol. The supplied degree schedule gives total root budget 48.
steps: Sum the twelve degree bounds: 12·4=48.
Require 48/|F|≤0.1, equivalently |F|≥480.
Among the listed primes only 487 meets this requirement; its bound is about 0.0986.
distractors: Correct: 487 exceeds 480, while field elements still have small binary descriptions.
The bound is 48/101, about 0.475, which is above the target.
The bound is 48/127, about 0.378, still above the target.
The raw sum bound exceeds one here and yields no useful target guarantee.
teaching.takeaway: Polynomially bounded degree is necessary, but the chosen field must also match the target error.
teaching.followup: If the number of checks doubles with the same degree bound, what field-size lower bound suffices?

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: Two hidden verifier tapes give the same visible transcript. Tape 0 has probability 3/4 and accepts only reply 0; tape 1 has probability 1/4 and accepts only reply 1. What is the best legal acceptance probability at this prover turn?
questions.skill: Maximize over an information set
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Maximize over an information set

teaching.summary: The prover must choose one reply for all hidden tapes consistent with its observation. It can choose reply 0 and win on the heavier tape, but cannot choose a different answer based on which hidden tape actually occurred.
steps: Reply 0 accepts with probability 3/4; reply 1 accepts with probability 1/4.
A randomized reply mixes these two values and cannot exceed their maximum.
Maximizing separately on each hidden tape would yield 1, but illegally reveals the tape to the prover.
distractors: This would be the value for equally weighted tapes; the given weights are unequal.
Correct: the single legal reply 0 achieves the larger weighted acceptance probability.
This allows the reply to depend on information hidden from the prover.
One legal reply succeeds on a positive-probability compatible tape, so zero is not optimal.
teaching.takeaway: Choose a strategy using the prover’s information, then average over hidden verifier randomness.
teaching.followup: Write the maximization outside the weighted sum and compare it with the illegal reversed order.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: A normalized verifier uses exactly 20 fair random bits. When its acceptance probability is evaluated exactly, what is the largest number of binary bits needed for the numerator of a fraction with denominator 2²⁰?
questions.skill: Bound the space of exact probabilities
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Bound the space of exact probabilities

teaching.summary: There are 2²⁰ equally likely random tapes. Counting accepting tapes gives an integer between 0 and 2²⁰ inclusive, and that integer has at most 21 bits. An exponential number of tapes therefore does not require an exponentially long probability numerator.
steps: Use the common denominator 2²⁰ fixed by the verifier’s random-tape length.
The numerator counts successful tapes and is at most 2²⁰.
The number 2²⁰ is 1 followed by twenty zeros in binary, requiring 21 positions.
distractors: No multiplication by a million appears; the representation length grows linearly with random-bit count.
This is the number of tapes, not the number of bits required to represent their count.
Correct: inclusive counting up to 2²⁰ requires at most 21 bits.
This confuses the numeric exponent with doubling the representation; a 21-bit numerator already suffices.
teaching.takeaway: Exponential enumeration and polynomial-size exact arithmetic are compatible.
teaching.followup: Generalize the numerator bit bound to a verifier using R(n) fair random bits.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: A depth-first protocol evaluation stores at most n² stack frames, each using at most 10n bits including its loop counters. What is the polynomial order of the resulting stack-space estimate, including another O(n) global workspace?
questions.skill: Account for stack space without confusing time
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Account for stack space without confusing time

teaching.summary: Space is the number of simultaneously stored bits. Depth-first evaluation reuses the workspace of a completed branch, so the number of branches affects time rather than the number of live frames. The stipulated stack bounds multiply.
steps: At most n² recursive frames are simultaneously live.
Each uses at most 10n bits, so the live stack requires at most 10n³ bits.
The additional O(n) global workspace is absorbed by O(n³), regardless of an exponential number of visited branches.
distractors: Exponential branching can produce exponential time, but does not force every branch to be stored together.
A stack with n² frames of linear size is not justified by logarithmic storage.
This counts one frame and omits the possible n² simultaneously live recursion levels.
Correct: polynomial depth times polynomial frame size gives this polynomial-space bound.
teaching.takeaway: To prove a space upper bound, count live storage rather than total work.
teaching.followup: How would the bound change if each frame stored an entire exponential list of compatible random tapes?

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: A first prover supplies values at eight indices. Three disagree with the fixed table supplied by an isolated second prover. A uniformly random one of the eight entries is checked. What is the rejection probability for this view?
questions.skill: Quantify a local consistency check
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Quantify a local consistency check

teaching.summary: Condition on the proposed eight-entry view and the second prover’s fixed answer function. Exactly three choices of the uniformly checked entry expose a disagreement. This local calculation alone does not establish that the global table encodes a valid witness.
steps: Name the eight possible checked positions and fix the proposed view before sampling one.
Three sampled positions produce unequal answers, so they force rejection.
Divide the number of disagreeing entries by all possible checked entries: 3/8.
distractors: Correct: the verifier detects exactly the three disagreements among eight equally likely positions.
Only one entry is sampled; introducing a second factor of eight does not match this experiment.
This would count only one disagreeing entry, whereas the view has three.
This is the probability of selecting one of the five agreeing entries and passing this check.
teaching.takeaway: A local consistency estimate measures agreement with one table, not satisfaction of all witness constraints.
teaching.followup: What check probability would result if the verifier sampled two entries independently with replacement?

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: Classical isolated provers share a random seed before a one-round protocol. Why may maximum-acceptance analysis consider a deterministic pair of response tables?
options: The verifier can read the shared seed.
Some fixed seed achieves acceptance at least the average over seeds.
Shared randomness must make their tables independent.
Every seed gives exactly the same acceptance probability.
questions.skill: Fix shared randomness without changing the model
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Fix shared randomness without changing the model
