teaching.summary: A shared seed may correlate the response tables. Conditioning on one seed fixes two deterministic functions, each of its own question. Acceptance with shared randomness is an average of the values of these fixed pairs, so one pair achieves at least that average.
steps: For each seed, write down both complete local response functions.
Evaluate the verifier’s acceptance probability for that fixed pair over its own random coins.
Average these values over seeds. A maximum is at least the average, yielding a sufficiently good deterministic pair.
distractors: The seed is fixed for analysis, not exposed to the verifier during the protocol.
Correct: averaging supplies a deterministic pair with at least the randomized strategy’s value.
Advance coordination can correlate the tables strongly; no-communication does not imply independence.
Different seeds can have different values; the argument needs only one attaining at least the average.
teaching.takeaway: Classical isolation restricts dependence on the other question, not advance coordination.
teaching.followup: Explain why the same argument does not authorize a prover to change its table after seeing the other prover’s question.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: The second prover is supposed to receive only an index i. A modified verifier also sends it the first prover’s full proposed view before asking for π(i). Which inference fails?
options: The verifier can compute the selected index.
A random index is still uniform.
The response can be treated as the value of one fixed table depending only on i.
Every polynomial has a multilinear extension.
questions.skill: Identify the information needed for oracle consistency
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Identify the information needed for oracle consistency

teaching.summary: The second prover can now tailor its answer to the particular proposed view. Different first-prover questions can induce different answers at the same index. The cross-check therefore no longer certifies agreement with a single fixed oracle.
steps: In the original experiment, the isolated answer is a function π(i) of the index alone.
With the extra message it may instead be π(i,view), so the same i can receive inconsistent answers across views.
Matching the displayed view is then possible without committing to one global witness table.
distractors: The verifier can still select and compute an index; the issue is what the prover learns.
Sampling can remain uniform while the prover’s information changes enough to invalidate soundness.
Correct: giving the surrounding view destroys the fixed-oracle interpretation used by the consistency proof.
Existence of a multilinear extension for a Boolean table is an algebraic fact unaffected by this message.
teaching.takeaway: Inspect the entire question each isolated prover sees before extracting an oracle from its strategy.
teaching.followup: Construct two proposed views that disagree at the same index, and show how this modified second prover can pass both.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: For P(X,Y,Z)=XYZ over F₁₀₁, compare its restriction to (t,1,1) with its restriction to (t,t,t). Which pair of degrees is correct?
questions.skill: Distinguish coordinate lines from general lines
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Distinguish coordinate lines from general lines

teaching.summary: Multilinearity bounds the degree in each coordinate separately. On a coordinate line only one variable changes, giving degree at most one. On a general affine line several variables vary together, so their degrees can add.
steps: Substitute (t,1,1) to obtain the univariate polynomial t.
Substitute (t,t,t) to obtain t³, which has degree three over the stated field.
The two line tests therefore need different promised-degree bounds, despite the same multivariate polynomial.
distractors: The first restriction is exactly t, so its degree is one rather than three.
The first restriction is not constant; its value changes with t.
The second line varies all three coordinates and gives t³, not an affine polynomial.
Correct: coordinate multilinearity and total degree produce different restriction degrees.
teaching.takeaway: “Multilinear” does not mean “affine on every line.”
teaching.followup: For a product of m distinct variables, find a line on which the restriction has degree m.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: An oracle is promised to be exactly a multilinear polynomial in four variables. To recover its value at a target using interpolation along a general line through that target, how many distinct nonzero parameter values suffice?
questions.skill: Count exact self-correction queries
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Count exact self-correction queries

teaching.summary: A four-variable multilinear polynomial has total degree at most four. Its restriction to a general affine line is therefore a univariate polynomial of degree at most four. Five distinct sampled parameters determine that polynomial and hence its value at parameter zero.
steps: Write the line as z+tv, with z the target and t=0 its parameter.
Substitution yields a univariate polynomial of degree at most four.
Evaluate at five distinct nonzero parameters and interpolate, assuming the field contains enough such parameters.
distractors: Correct: degree at most four requires five distinct evaluations for exact interpolation.
Sixteen is the number of Boolean table entries, not the number needed for one degree-four line restriction.
Two points determine an affine restriction, but a general line here can have degree four.
Four samples do not uniquely determine an arbitrary degree-four polynomial.
teaching.takeaway: Exact self-correction uses the degree of the sampled restriction, not the Boolean table’s size.
teaching.followup: Which part of this argument fails if a small fraction of the oracle’s answers is corrupted?

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: An arbitrary table passes most of a protocol’s multilinearity tests. Before applying exact polynomial interpolation as if the table were a polynomial, what must still be established?
options: That the witness length is polynomial.
A quantitative proximity/decoding theorem relating test acceptance to one global polynomial.
That the table is exactly affine on every general line.
That every tested point is correct with probability one.
questions.skill: Name the robust testing theorem
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Name the robust testing theorem

teaching.summary: Interpolation is an algebraic statement about a promised low-degree polynomial. A table that merely passes many local checks lacks that promise. BFL needs a robust theorem connecting test acceptance, global proximity, and correction error; this is a substantive proof obligation.
steps: Separate the actual input to the tester, an arbitrary function, from an ideal multilinear polynomial.
State the proximity conclusion and its dependence on rejection probability and field parameters.
Use the resulting global polynomial and a noise analysis before composing interpolation with consistency checks.
distractors: BFL is designed to check an exponentially long witness using short queries; polynomial witness length is not required.
Correct: the robust global implication is the missing bridge from local tests to a usable polynomial.
A multilinear polynomial may have degree greater than one on a general line.
High acceptance permits some errors and does not make every queried answer correct.
teaching.takeaway: Do not use a promise that the test is supposed to establish as an assumption in its soundness proof.
teaching.followup: State separately what exact interpolation proves and what the multilinearity proximity theorem must prove.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: In a one-round classical protocol, each prover receives an n-bit question and returns n² bits. How large is one complete deterministic response table?
questions.skill: Count a prover strategy table
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Count a prover strategy table

teaching.summary: There are 2ⁿ possible questions and one n²-bit answer for each. Writing the table uses exponential space in n if stored in full, but a nondeterministic exponential-time upper-bound simulation is allowed to guess and access such an exponentially long object.
steps: Enumerate all n-bit question strings: there are 2ⁿ rows.
Place one n²-bit answer in each row, producing 2ⁿ·n² bits total.
For a fixed number of provers the total remains singly exponential, which fits the strategy-guessing upper bound.
distractors: This stores only one answer and omits the response to every other question.
This counts only polynomially many questions, although n-bit questions have 2ⁿ possible values.
Correct: multiply the number of question strings by the answer length.
This counts a much larger quantity and confuses the number of possible tables with one table’s length.
teaching.takeaway: Distinguish a strategy’s description length from the number of possible strategies.
teaching.followup: How many distinct response tables of this format exist, and why is that a different question?

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: A computation tableau has 2^(n²) locations. How many bits suffice to address one location, and what does that imply about reading the whole tableau?
options: n² bits; therefore a complete scan takes n² steps.
2^(n²) bits; therefore the verifier must use exponential-length questions.
n bits; therefore the whole tableau is polynomial.
n² bits; short addresses do not make a complete scan polynomial.
questions.skill: Separate address length from witness length
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Separate address length from witness length

teaching.summary: An exponentially long object can have polynomial-length addresses. This makes local querying possible, but does not let a polynomial-time verifier inspect all entries. Algebraic encoding and testing are needed to extract a global guarantee from a few local observations.
steps: Index the locations by binary integers from 0 to 2^(n²)−1.
Each such index needs n² bits, even though there are exponentially many locations.
A complete scan still takes at least one step per location, so short indexing alone is not the verification theorem.
distractors: This converts a representation-length bound into an unsupported running-time bound for the full scan.
The binary logarithm of the number of locations determines address length, not the number itself.
n bits address only 2ⁿ locations and are insufficient for this larger tableau.
Correct: polynomial addresses support short queries, while global verification remains a separate difficulty.
teaching.takeaway: Short access is an interface to a long witness, not a substitute for checking its consistency.
teaching.followup: Name the three ingredients that connect isolated local answers to a valid encoded computation in BFL.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: A soundness composition has three bad events with probability bounds 0.02, 0.03, and 0.04, and acceptance of a false statement implies at least one bad event. Which is the strongest acceptance bound obtained by adding these estimates without assuming independence?
questions.skill: Compose testing, consistency, and algebraic errors
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Compose testing, consistency, and algebraic errors

teaching.summary: The acceptance event is contained in a union of failure events. The probability of a union is at most the sum of the marginal bounds, even when the events are correlated. The result is an upper bound, not a claim that all budgets are attained.
steps: Identify the logical implication from false acceptance to a testing, consistency, or algebraic failure.
Apply the union bound to those three events rather than assuming independence.
Add the budgets to obtain at most 0.09; overlap can make the actual probability smaller.
distractors: Correct: 0.02+0.03+0.04 is a valid upper bound under the stated containment.
A product would bound an intersection under additional assumptions, not this union.
The union can be smaller because events overlap or their individual bounds are loose.
The maximum individual bound does not control a union of different possible failures.
teaching.takeaway: A composed verifier needs both a logical error decomposition and numerical budgets for every term.
teaching.followup: Give an example of overlapping events for which the sum bound is strict.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: A graph on four vertices has exactly two automorphisms. Choose a uniformly random permutation of its vertex labels. How many distinct labeled copies arise, and what is the probability of each?
questions.skill: Compute a relabeling transcript distribution
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Compute a relabeling transcript distribution

teaching.summary: Two permutations produce the same labeled graph exactly when they differ by an automorphism. Each labeled copy has the same number of preimages. This uniformity underlies the honest graph-isomorphism transcript calculation.
steps: There are 4!=24 possible label permutations.
Each labeled copy is produced by exactly two permutations, one for each automorphism.
There are 24/2=12 copies, each occurring with probability 2/24=1/12.
distractors: Two is the number of permutations per copy, not the number of distinct copies.
Correct: equal automorphism fibers yield 12 equally likely labeled copies.
Every copy has the same two-permutation fiber, so its probability cannot vary with the copy.
Different label permutations can produce the same graph when it has nontrivial automorphisms.
teaching.takeaway: Transcript simulation requires the distribution of outputs, including multiplicities of the random choices.
teaching.followup: Why do two isomorphic input graphs induce the same distribution of uniformly relabeled graphs?

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: Two interactions always output the same final accept bit, but one transcript also reveals a witness-dependent bit. Is equality of the accept-bit distributions enough for zero knowledge?
options: Yes, if the honest prover accepts with certainty.
No: zero knowledge requires the verifier to reject.
No: the simulated and real full verifier views must be compared.
Yes: acceptance is the only output the definition observes.
questions.skill: Compare full views rather than one marginal
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Compare full views rather than one marginal

teaching.summary: A verifier learns from the messages and its internal state, not just its final decision. Matching the acceptance marginal can conceal a transcript difference that leaks information. The simulator requirement is a statement about the complete prescribed view.
steps: Specify the view, including auxiliary input, random tape, and received messages.
Projecting a view onto its accept bit can discard the very information that distinguishes the interactions.
Compare the full distributions with the required perfect, statistical, or computational notion.
distractors: Perfect completeness constrains acceptance on true statements, not what the verifier learns.
A convincing zero-knowledge proof should accept true statements; rejection is not its privacy condition.
Correct: an extra witness-dependent message must be accounted for by the simulation definition.
This replaces the full-view definition by an insufficient one-bit marginal.
teaching.takeaway: Completeness, soundness, and zero knowledge control different properties of one interaction.
teaching.followup: Construct two simple distributions with the same final bit but disjoint full transcript supports.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: An honest-verifier graph-isomorphism simulator samples the challenge bit independently of the first graph. A cheating verifier instead chooses that bit as a function of the first graph. What remains to be proved?
options: That independently sampled challenge bits still automatically match the cheating view.
That the honest verifier’s random coins were uniform.
A simulator and running-time analysis for this arbitrary verifier strategy.
questions.skill: Distinguish honest-verifier and full zero knowledge
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Distinguish honest-verifier and full zero knowledge

teaching.summary: The honest transcript factorization used an independent uniform challenge. Changing the verifier can change that dependence. A full zero-knowledge argument supplies a simulator for each efficient cheating verifier and analyzes its entire output distribution and expected running time.
steps: Identify the independence assumption in the honest-verifier transcript generation.
Observe that the cheating verifier may correlate its challenge with the first message and auxiliary input.
Provide a separate simulation strategy, with justified guessing or rewinding if used, rather than reusing the honest law unchanged.
distractors: The data representation of a graph does not address the changed challenge distribution.
This is the unproved assertion: independent sampling can erase a correlation present in the real view.
The honest verifier’s coins may already be uniform; the new adversarial strategy is the obstacle.
Correct: simulation must cover that verifier and establish both its distributional guarantee and efficiency.
teaching.takeaway: An honest-verifier simulator is a useful calculation, not by itself a proof against all verifiers.
teaching.followup: Which parts of the view must be restored when a simulator rewinds a cheating verifier?

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: In the hidden-bit graph experiment, G₀ and G₁ are isomorphic and b is fair. After seeing a uniformly relabeled copy of G_b, what is the maximum probability that any prover correctly guesses b?
questions.skill: Derive hidden-bit soundness from identical laws
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Derive hidden-bit soundness from identical laws

teaching.summary: Isomorphic graphs have the same distribution under uniform relabeling. The received graph therefore supplies no information about the fair hidden bit. Even an unbounded prover cannot improve on guessing in this false-instance experiment.
steps: For every labeled graph H, its conditional probability is identical under b=0 and b=1.
Bayes’ rule consequently leaves the posterior hidden bit uniform wherever H has positive probability.
Any deterministic or randomized response succeeds with probability at most 1/2; a fixed guess attains it.
distractors: Correct: identical conditional laws preserve the fair prior and give soundness one half.
A fixed guess already succeeds on one of the two equally probable hidden-bit values.
Perfect guessing would require a distinction between the two identical challenge distributions.
This would require a posterior bias not supplied by the received graph.
teaching.takeaway: Information-theoretic soundness can hold against an unbounded prover.
teaching.followup: Explain why the same experiment has perfect completeness when the two graphs are nonisomorphic.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: Repeat the hidden-bit test sequentially five times on isomorphic graphs, using fresh independent fair hidden bits, and accept only if every answer is right. What is the sharpest listed soundness bound supplied by multiplying the five conditional one-half estimates?
questions.skill: Amplify using conditional soundness
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Amplify using conditional soundness

teaching.summary: Past transcripts can influence the prover’s future strategy, but each fresh challenge still hides an unbiased bit on isomorphic inputs. Conditional on any successful history, the next success probability is at most one half. The five factors therefore multiply.
steps: Condition on the entire interaction before the next fresh round.
The two next-round challenge laws are identical, so conditional success remains at most 1/2.
Apply this bound five times to the event of success in every round, yielding 2⁻⁵=1/32.

Correct: fresh conditional one-half bounds give at most one successful all-round transcript in probability 2⁻⁵.

teaching.followup: What can go wrong if the verifier reuses the same hidden bit and relabeled graph in every round?

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: A claimed full zero-knowledge proof for graph nonisomorphism only simulates challenges honestly generated as random copies of G₀ or G₁. Which adversarial case is still missing?
options: A cheating verifier sending an arbitrary graph not certified to come from that experiment.
A verifier choosing a different uniform permutation of the same inputs.

questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Locate the GMW challenge-certification obligation

An arbitrary challenge may ask the prover to reveal isomorphism information outside that experiment. The complete GMW construction needs its challenge-certification and simulation argument.
steps: State exactly which challenge distribution the proposed simulator reproduces.
Allow an efficient cheating verifier to choose a graph and auxiliary information by another rule.
Explain how certification and its simulator handle that rule; hidden-bit soundness alone does not do so.

teaching.followup: Name the two separate claims proved by the hidden-bit exchange and by challenge certification.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: For a non-3-colorable graph with ten edges, assume ideal binding commitments and twenty sequential fresh-edge challenges. Which is the bound computed by multiplying the twenty conditional estimates obtained from one rejecting edge per round?
questions.skill: Derive commitment-based soundness amplification
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Derive commitment-based soundness amplification

teaching.summary: Binding fixes the colors before the edge challenge. Any invalid committed coloring has a rejecting edge, so one uniform edge challenge accepts with probability at most 9/10. The conditional probability of passing a round is therefore at most 1−1/10.
Passing all twenty rounds has probability at most (9/10)²⁰, approximately 0.1216.

teaching.takeaway: A weak but explicit one-round gap can be amplified, with the commitment convention kept attached.
teaching.followup: How many sequential rounds suffice to make the bound at most e⁻³ using (1−1/m)^t≤e⁻ᵗᐟᵐ?

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: Fix an edge whose endpoints have distinct colors in a proper 3-coloring. After a uniform permutation of the three color names, what is the probability that its ordered endpoint colors are exactly (red,blue)?
questions.skill: Compute the local opening distribution
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Compute the local opening distribution

teaching.summary: There are six permutations of the three color names. Each sends the two original distinct endpoint colors to one ordered distinct pair, and every such pair occurs once. The local distribution is uniform on six pairs, never on all nine pairs.
steps: Count the possible ordered distinct pairs: three choices for the first color and two for the second.
A color permutation sending the two endpoint colors to a specified pair uniquely determines the third color’s image.
Thus one of the six equally likely permutations yields (red,blue), giving probability 1/6.

This leaves out the distinction between the three possible first colors.
This counts only the first endpoint’s marginal and omits the required second color.
Independent uniform endpoint colors would permit equality, unlike a relabeled proper edge.
teaching.takeaway: Simulation must preserve correlations; matching two separate uniform marginals is insufficient.
teaching.followup: Why does this six-pair calculation not by itself prove simulation of all unopened commitments?

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: Suppose commitments hide colors perfectly but allow the prover to open each commitment to any color after seeing the challenged edge. What fails in the coloring protocol’s soundness proof?
options: No fixed global coloring is committed before the challenge.
The hidden colors necessarily become visible before the challenge.
The verifier can no longer choose a uniform edge.
questions.skill: Separate binding from hiding
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: Separate binding from hiding

teaching.summary: Hiding limits what the verifier learns. Binding limits how the prover can change a committed value. If the prover can choose openings after seeing the edge, it can make that one edge look properly colored without possessing one globally proper assignment.
steps: The usual soundness argument first extracts one fixed color for every committed vertex.
Equivocal commitments remove that fixed-assignment premise; the openings can depend on which edge is requested.
The prover can then answer locally with two distinct colors on every challenge, even if no global coloring exists.
distractors: A cheating local opening does not change the graph’s true colorability.
Correct: soundness needs binding to connect different possible openings to one prechallenge assignment.
Perfect hiding can still hold; the defect is the prover’s ability to change openings.

teaching.followup: Explain the opposite failure mode: binding commitments that reveal every vertex color.

questions.subject: complexity

questions.question: On the two-point lattice let α=(1,2), β=(3,4), γ₁=4 and δ₀=2. What is the smallest possible (γ₀+γ₁)(δ₀+δ₁) satisfying all Four Functions hypotheses?
questions.skill: Optimize the one-coordinate inequality
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

The cross products are α₀β₁=4 and α₁β₀=6, both bounded by γ₁δ₀=8.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: In the two-point proof C=γ₁δ₀ is zero. Which repair correctly handles the apparent division by C?
options: Cancel C formally because both sides are continuous.
Assume γ₁ and δ₀ are positive without loss of generality.
The cross products vanish; add the diagonal bounds without dividing.
Discard the zero-coordinate case from the theorem.

Zero values are explicitly allowed, so positivity cannot simply be assumed.

teaching.followup: Explain exactly where nonnegativity is used in this repair.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: Let A={∅,{1},{2}} and B={{1}}. For pointwise union and intersection families, what is |A∨B|·|A∧B|?
questions.skill: Distinguish a family from a multiset
questions.readingLabel: Worked example: union/intersection families

teaching.summary: Union and intersection are applied to pairs of sets, but their resulting families contain each distinct set only once. Several input pairs can have the same output, so an injectivity argument is unavailable.

The intersection outputs are ∅, {1}, and ∅, again giving two distinct members.

teaching.followup: Replace the indicators by nonuniform nonnegative weights and identify the local hypothesis.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: Give 00 and 11 weight 1 each, and 01 and 10 weight 3 each. For the two increasing coordinate events, what is their covariance after normalization?

questions.readingLabel: Limits & counterexamples: the measure hypothesis

teaching.summary: Increasing events alone do not force positive correlation. This measure favors disagreement, and it fails the FKG lattice condition on the incomparable points 01 and 10.

The intersection event is 11, whose probability is 1/8.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: A nonnegative lattice weight μ satisfies μ(A)μ(B)≤μ(A∪B)μ(A∩B). If every weight is multiplied by c>0 and then normalized, what changes?
options: The probability measure and its correlations stay the same.
The lattice inequality reverses when c<1.
Every covariance becomes c² times as large.
The measure becomes a product measure.
questions.skill: Separate weights from normalized probabilities
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: The lattice condition is homogeneous of degree two, and normalization divides out the common scale. Changing units of mass does not change the underlying probability law or turn dependence into independence.

The new probability of A is cμ(A)/(c∑μ)=μ(A)/∑μ.
Every expectation under the normalized law is therefore unchanged, including covariance.
distractors: The common multiplier cancels exactly upon normalization.
Both sides receive the same positive multiplier c².

teaching.followup: Write the Four Functions proof first for weights and then perform the final normalization.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: An FKG proof handles nonnegative increasing functions, but increasing f and g may take negative values. What extends the covariance conclusion to finite real-valued f,g?
options: Replace each function by its absolute value.
Drop configurations where either function is negative.
Multiply f and g by their minima.
Add constants making both functions nonnegative; covariance is unchanged.
questions.skill: Extend a hypothesis without changing the target
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: On a finite lattice each function has a finite minimum. Adding sufficiently large constants preserves increasingness and makes the Four Functions application legal, while covariance ignores additive constants.

Apply the established FKG conclusion to these shifted functions.

teaching.followup: Verify Cov(f+a,g+b)=Cov(f,g) by expansion.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: Let X₁~Bernoulli(1/4) and X₂~Bernoulli(1/2) be independent. Set A={X₁=1}, B={X₁=1 or X₂=1}. What is Cov(1_A,1_B)?
questions.skill: Calculate the product-measure covariance
questions.readingLabel: Worked example: conditional event probabilities

teaching.summary: The containment A⊆B makes the intersection easy, but the covariance also requires the marginal of B. The two indicators are positively correlated without being independent.
steps: The complement of B requires X₁=0 and X₂=0, so Pr(B)=1−(3/4)(1/2)=5/8.
Because A implies B, Pr(A∩B)=Pr(A)=1/4.
The covariance is 1/4−(1/4)(5/8)=3/32.
distractors: This is the joint probability minus the product of marginals.
One-quarter is the intersection probability before the subtraction.
Five thirty-seconds is the product of the marginals, not their covariance.
The event containment creates a strict correlation in this nondegenerate example.
teaching.takeaway: Containment simplifies intersections, but does not replace the covariance calculation.
teaching.followup: Recover the same number using the conditional-mean covariance identity.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: In G(n,m), can the product-measure induction for Harris be used unchanged after conditioning on one edge?
options: Yes, because every graph has equal probability.
No: fixing the total number of edges couples the remaining edge indicators.
Yes, because every increasing graph event is independent.
No, because increasing events cannot be defined in G(n,m).

teaching.summary: Harris induction needs the conditional slice to remain a smaller product space. In G(n,m), learning that one edge is present changes how many of the remaining edges may be present, so that induction hypothesis is unavailable.
steps: In G(n,p), independent unrevealed edges retain their original Bernoulli distribution after one exposure.
In G(n,m), a present exposed edge leaves exactly m−1 present edges among the other coordinates.
Uniformity on a constrained set is not the same as independence of its coordinates.
distractors: Uniformity over graphs of a fixed size does not imply coordinate independence.

teaching.followup: For two potential edges with exactly one present, compute the covariance of their presence events.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: Under a product measure, A is increasing and B is decreasing. Which inequality follows from Harris by using Bᶜ?
questions.skill: Change monotonicity through complements
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: The complement of a decreasing event is increasing, so the positive-correlation theorem applies to A and Bᶜ. Rearranging its conclusion reverses the comparison for A and B.

Replace the left side by Pr(A)−Pr(A∩B) and the right side by Pr(A)(1−Pr(B)).
Cancel Pr(A) and multiply by negative one, reversing the inequality.

Opposite monotonicity does not imply independence.

teaching.takeaway: Complementing an event can convert a new sign pattern into a known theorem.
teaching.followup: Give a two-bit example with strict inequality and another with equality.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: On three unconstrained elements a,b,c, let A={a precedes b} and B={a precedes c} in a uniform ranking. What is Pr(A∩Bᶜ)?
questions.skill: Enumerate the shared-pivot events
questions.readingLabel: Worked example: enumerate linear extensions

teaching.summary: A∩Bᶜ requires c before a before b. There is exactly one such ranking among six, illustrating that pivot comparisons are dependent even in an unconstrained random permutation.
steps: A fixes a before b, while Bᶜ fixes c before a.
Together these impose the unique chain c<a<b.
Each of the six permutations is equally likely, so the probability is one-sixth.

One-quarter incorrectly multiplies probabilities of dependent comparisons.
One-half is the probability of just one comparison event.
Only the ranking c,a,b satisfies both required comparisons.
teaching.takeaway: Comparison indicators sharing a pivot are not independent.
teaching.followup: Compute Pr(A∩B) and compare its one-third with the marginal product one-quarter.

questions.question: A poset requires b<c, while a is incomparable with both. In a uniform linear extension, what are Pr(a<b) and Pr(a<c)?
questions.skill: Condition a ranking on a partial order
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: The valid extensions are a,b,c; b,a,c; and b,c,a. Uniformity is over these three extensions, not all six permutations, and the imposed order makes the two pivot marginals unequal.
steps: List the three positions in which a can be inserted into the fixed chain b<c.
Only the first extension places a before b, so that probability is one-third.
The first two extensions place a before c, so that probability is two-thirds.
distractors: The explicit extension counts give these two unequal marginals.
This would ignore the constraint b<c when using permutation symmetry.
This reverses the containment {a<b}⊆{a<c}.
It misses the valid extension b,a,c for the second event.
teaching.takeaway: Compute probabilities in the constrained extension space actually being sampled.
teaching.followup: Check that the intersection probability one-third exceeds the product two-ninths.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: Why is “apply Harris because the ranking is random” not a proof of the XYZ inequality for an arbitrary poset?
options: A uniform linear extension has dependent order constraints and needs the poset counting argument.
The XYZ events have probability zero.
Every random permutation is already a product measure on pairwise comparisons.
questions.skill: Locate the structural input
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: A distribution can be uniform and still have strongly dependent coordinates. Pairwise order comparisons satisfy transitivity and are additionally conditioned by the poset, so the independent-coordinate induction cannot simply be imported.
steps: Even for three unconstrained elements, the three pairwise comparisons cannot form a cyclic orientation.
A poset removes further rankings, changing conditional distributions of the remaining comparisons.
The assigned XYZ theorem uses its own structural argument for counts of linear extensions.
distractors: Harris is a product-space theorem, not a graph-only statement.
This identifies the missing hypothesis and the needed replacement theorem.
Many pivot events have positive probability, as small antichains already show.

teaching.takeaway: Randomness is not a substitute for checking a theorem’s sampling hypotheses.
teaching.followup: Explain how an imposed order relation changes the sample space without changing uniformity.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: Reveal six independent fair bits and use the Doob martingale for their sum. With |Dᵢ|≤1/2, which expression results from direct substitution into the stated one-sided Azuma formula for a deviation at least 3/2?

teaching.summary: The bounded-increment convention squares the centered increment, not the full replacement effect. Its upper bound is an exponential probability estimate; it is not the exponent alone.

The squared-increment sum is six times one-quarter, namely 3/2.

This exponent is too large for the specified bounded-increment convention.
This corresponds to a different or incorrectly aggregated increment bound.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: Which step makes the Azuma MGF proof work even when the martingale increments are dependent?
options: Replace all increments by independent copies.
Assert that zero covariance implies independence.
Apply a conditional exponential bound and the tower property at every step.
Factor the unconditional MGF into a product without conditioning.

questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: A martingale gives a zero conditional mean, and the increment bound supplies a conditional MGF estimate valid for every history. Iterating conditional expectations is enough; unconditional factorization is generally false.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: A mean-zero variable has variance one but equals 100 and −100 with probability 1/20000 each. Why cannot variance alone justify the Azuma estimate exp(−t²/2)?
options: The claimed upper tail at t=100 would be far smaller than its actual probability.
A mean-zero variable cannot have atoms.
Azuma never applies to finite probability spaces.
questions.skill: Distinguish variance from maximum effect
questions.readingLabel: Limits & counterexamples: bounded jumps versus variance

teaching.summary: Small second moment permits very rare large jumps. Azuma’s exponential tail requires a deterministic bound on each increment, not merely a variance estimate with the same numerical value.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: Let P(G) be the largest number of edge-disjoint triangles in G. Which sharp bound holds when one edge is deleted?
options: The decrease is at most one, and one is attained.

questions.skill: Choose a low-sensitivity auxiliary variable

teaching.summary: An edge-disjoint packing uses an edge in at most one packed triangle. Removing that one affected triangle leaves a valid packing in the modified graph; compare optimal packings in both directions.

If the deleted edge occurs in the packing, discard its unique packed triangle; otherwise discard nothing.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: Two graphs differ only in edges incident to one vertex v. Why do their chromatic numbers differ by at most one?
options: The changed edges all share one color.
Deleting v leaves the same graph, and adding v needs at most one fresh color.
Every graph is three-colorable after deleting one vertex.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: The assigned sparse chromatic result uses p=n⁻ᵅ with fixed α>5/6 and a window [u,u+3]. Which interpretation is correct?
options: It proves four-integer concentration for every p.
It places χ in at most three possible integer values.
Azuma alone gives this window without structural input.

teaching.summary: The endpoints u and u+3 include four integers. The sparse regime and the structural coloring estimate are part of the statement and proof; neither can be removed because a related concentration theorem exists.
steps: List the integer values u, u+1, u+2, and u+3.
Retain the fixed parameter assumption α>5/6 when substituting p=n⁻ᵅ.
Distinguish the martingale ingredient from the extra sparse-graph structure that sharpens its window.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: Query four independent Bernoulli(0.2) bits until the first 1 or until all four are read. If each query is charged variance cost 0.16, which is the smallest valid pathwise cumulative bound among these choices?

teaching.summary: The adaptive theorem’s budget must cover every legal query path. Some histories require reading all four bits, so the maximum cost is four times 0.16, even though the expected cost is smaller.
steps: The histories 0000 and 0001 require four queries and have positive probability.
No history makes more than four queries, so the maximum cumulative charge is 4·0.16=0.64.
The expected query count is 1+0.8+0.8²+0.8³=2.952, producing the different average charge 0.47232.

teaching.followup: Why does positive probability of the all-zero history matter for this check?

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: For an integrable terminal variable Y and an increasing information sequence Fᵢ, why is Mᵢ=E[Y|Fᵢ] a martingale?
options: All future queries are chosen in advance.
Every conditional expectation equals the terminal value.
Y must be a sum of independent indicators.
questions.skill: Build the martingale before its concentration bound
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: The Doob construction depends on nested information and integrability. It does not need a predetermined exposure order or an additive terminal variable; bounded increments are a subsequent, separate obligation.
steps: Mᵢ is measurable with respect to the information available at stage i.
Because Fᵢ₋₁ is contained in Fᵢ, iterated conditioning collapses E[E[Y|Fᵢ]|Fᵢ₋₁] to E[Y|Fᵢ₋₁].
This verifies the martingale identity, but gives no numerical increment bound by itself.
distractors: Nested conditioning proves exactly the required martingale identity.
Adaptive query selection is compatible with the Doob construction.
The terminal value is known only when enough information has been revealed.
Integrability and a filtration suffice for this identity.
teaching.takeaway: The existence of a martingale and a useful tail estimate are distinct steps.
teaching.followup: Give an adaptive exposure whose martingale has a much larger increment bound than its variance suggests.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: An adaptive-query proof checks a maximum-effect bound only along its most likely path. What is missing?
options: A bound on all legal histories to which the theorem applies.
A proof that every query has the same answer.
A uniform distribution over query trees.
A claim that small conditional variance forces a small maximum jump.
questions.skill: Quantify over the whole query strategy
questions.readingLabel: Limits & counterexamples: maximum effect

teaching.summary: A rare legal history can contain the large increment that invalidates the desired tail estimate. A theorem with a pathwise effect hypothesis must be checked on every relevant history, not merely on typical execution traces.
steps: Specify the conditional law of the next queried coordinate after each history.
Bound how far the target conditional expectation can move under every allowed answer.
Combine these bounds with the cumulative conditional-variance requirement in the theorem’s permitted parameter range.
distractors: The maximum-effect condition is a uniform obligation over legal paths.
Different query answers are the reason a branching process must be analyzed.
The strategy may be deterministic; uniform random selection of a tree is not required.
Small variance permits rare large jumps and cannot replace the missing condition.
teaching.takeaway: Adaptive concentration requires conditional checks, including rare branches.
teaching.followup: Construct a two-branch process whose rare branch has a large jump.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: Throw balls into bins and let Z count empty bins. Moving one ball from one bin to another changes Z by at most what?
questions.skill: Exploit cancellation in a coordinate change
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: Only the old and new bins can change emptiness. When both statuses change, one becomes empty while the other stops being empty, and their effects cancel instead of adding.
steps: Removing the ball can increase Z by one only if its old bin becomes empty.
Adding the ball can decrease Z by one only if its new bin was empty.
The possible combined changes are −1, 0, and 1, giving absolute effect at most one.
distractors: A ball moved from a multiply occupied bin to an empty bin reduces Z by one.
The two possible status changes have opposite signs.
This adds absolute changes and misses their cancellation in the target count.
Only two bins are touched, and the signed count is even less sensitive.
teaching.takeaway: Analyze the signed change in the target, not just the number of coordinates touched.
teaching.followup: Use identical future ball placements to turn this replacement bound into a Doob increment bound.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: Let f(ε)=||Σᵢεᵢvᵢ|| with ||vᵢ||≤1. What is the sharpest universal full replacement-effect bound among these choices when one sign εⱼ is flipped?
questions.skill: State the full replacement effect
questions.readingLabel: Definitions & theorem: sensitivity conventions

teaching.summary: Flipping a sign changes the sum vector by twice that vector. The reverse triangle inequality then controls the change in its norm. A centered martingale convention can yield a different numerical bound and must be stated separately.
steps: The changed vector sum differs by −2εⱼvⱼ.
Its norm is at most 2||vⱼ||≤2.
The reverse triangle inequality bounds the absolute change in f by that vector difference.
distractors: One-half is not a general replacement bound for this norm function.
A one-dimensional single-vector example changes by two for suitable additional terms.
This follows directly from the vector replacement and reverse triangle inequality.
Four overcounts the factor from flipping one sign.
teaching.takeaway: Distinguish full function sensitivity from a centered conditional-increment convention.
teaching.followup: Explain when fair-sign conditioning can improve the associated martingale constant.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: For nonempty A in the binary cube, let d(x,A) be ordinary Hamming distance to A. If x and x′ differ in one bit, what must hold?
options: The difference can be the cube dimension.
questions.skill: Transfer a metric inequality to a minimum
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: Distance to a fixed set is one-Lipschitz in any metric. Compare distances to each candidate point of A and then minimize; changing which point is nearest does not invalidate the bound.
steps: For each a∈A, the metric triangle inequality gives d(x,a)≤1+d(x′,a).
Choose a nearest point to x′ to obtain d(x,A)≤1+d(x′,A).
Interchange x and x′ to bound the opposite difference as well.
distractors: Neighboring cube points can have distances zero and one from a singleton set.
The two triangle-inequality comparisons give this absolute bound.
Minimization over A cannot amplify a one-coordinate metric change this way.
The distances depend on A and can be zero or much larger than one.
teaching.takeaway: A nearest-point choice may change, but distance-to-set remains Lipschitz.
teaching.followup: Use this bound to define an exposure martingale for d(X,A).

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: For A={000,111} and x=001, mismatch vectors are (0,0,1) and (1,1,0). What is their minimum convex-hull Euclidean norm?
questions.skill: Calculate convex rather than Hamming distance
questions.readingLabel: Worked example: convex mismatch geometry

teaching.summary: A convex combination can spread mismatches over coordinates. Minimize its squared norm, not the Hamming count of a single witness; the optimizing combination need not be the equally weighted midpoint.
steps: Give weight t to (0,0,1) and 1−t to (1,1,0), obtaining (1−t,1−t,t).
Its squared norm is 2(1−t)²+t², minimized at t=2/3.
The minimum squared norm is 2/3, so the distance is √(2/3), below the Hamming distance one.
distractors: One is the closest individual mismatch norm, before convexification.
Two-thirds is the minimum squared norm rather than the distance.
The quadratic minimization yields this norm exactly.
Square root of three is the all-mismatch norm and is not a minimum.
teaching.takeaway: Convexification optimizes combinations of witnesses, not only individual witnesses.
teaching.followup: Find the optimal weights when the two mismatch supports have sizes r and s.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: Suppose μ(A)=1/4 and E exp(d_T(X,A)²/4)≤1/μ(A). What is the smallest listed upper bound on Pr(d_T(X,A)≥4) supplied by exponential Markov using this estimate?
questions.skill: Derive a tail from the exponential moment
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: Markov’s inequality applies to the nonnegative exponential of squared distance. The event distance at least four forces this exponential to be at least e⁴, and the reciprocal event mass remains in the numerator.
steps: At d_T≥4 the random variable exp(d_T²/4) is at least exp(16/4)=e⁴.
Its expectation is bounded by 1/μ(A)=4.
Markov therefore gives the upper bound 4/e⁴; it does not remove the factor depending on μ(A).
distractors: This omits the factor 1/μ(A) from the given moment estimate.
The moment numerator is four and the threshold denominator is e⁴.
This uses the wrong squared-distance exponent.
One-quarter is the mass of A, not the derived distance-tail bound.
teaching.takeaway: Keep the set-mass factor when converting a product-space inequality to a tail.
teaching.followup: For general μ(A)=a and threshold u, derive the corresponding expression.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: A proof replaces Talagrand’s convex distance by ordinary Hamming distance because both count mismatches. What is wrong?
options: The two distances are always equal.
Ordinary Hamming distance is undefined on the binary cube.
Talagrand requires convex combinations or weighted mismatch geometry, which can give a different value.
The probability measure must be uniform for either distance to exist.
questions.skill: Preserve the distance in the theorem
questions.readingLabel: Limits & counterexamples: the meaning of convex distance

teaching.summary: The convex distance is designed to aggregate several ways of reaching an event. Hamming distance uses the number of changed coordinates for one point. Interchanging them changes the hypothesis-to-tail connection and can make the quoted inequality false.
steps: For A={00,11} and x=01, the closest Hamming distance is one.
The two mismatch vectors (0,1) and (1,0) have midpoint (1/2,1/2), whose norm is 1/√2.
A theorem for one quantity cannot be re-labeled as a theorem for the larger, different quantity without another comparison argument.
distractors: The two-point example gives distinct values and disproves equality.
Hamming distance is the standard metric of the binary cube.
The specific geometry is an essential part of the statement.
The metric definitions do not require a uniform probability law.
teaching.takeaway: Do not replace a theorem’s geometric quantity by an intuitively similar one.
teaching.followup: Explain why d_T≤√d_H does not transfer the same upper-tail estimate to d_H.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: For maximum matching size X on a graph with 100 vertices, a fixed matching of seven present edges certifies X≥7. How many edge coordinates must that certificate reveal?
questions.skill: Count certificate coordinates
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: The certificate consists of the seven edge-presence facts, together with the deterministic observation that their endpoints are disjoint. Revealing every other possible edge is unnecessary because no completion removes the displayed matching.
steps: Specify seven pairwise vertex-disjoint edges and reveal that each is present.
Every assignment of the unrevealed edge coordinates still contains these seven matching edges.
Thus seven coordinates suffice, whereas fourteen counts vertices and 4950 counts all potential edges.
distractors: The seven present edge indicators already force the desired lower bound.
Fourteen counts endpoints, but the random coordinates here are edge indicators.
Forty-nine is not the number of edge facts used by this witness.
The whole graph is unnecessary for certifying one concrete matching.
teaching.takeaway: A certificate must force the claim under every completion of unrevealed coordinates.
teaching.followup: Why does seven-edge presence without vertex-disjointness fail to certify a seven-edge matching?

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: For maximum matching size, certifiability uses f(b)=b. At b=100, which absolute deficit corresponds to t=2 in the bound Pr(X≤b−t√f(b))Pr(X≥b)≤exp(−t²/4)?
questions.skill: Read the certificate concentration scale
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: The square root applies to certificate size, not to the total number of possible edges. With a 100-edge certificate, the theorem compares values separated by twenty when the dimensionless parameter is two.
steps: Evaluate f(100)=100 and its square root, ten.
Multiply by t=2 to obtain absolute deficit twenty and lower threshold eighty.
The corresponding product of event probabilities is bounded by exp(−1), not yet a one-sided bound by itself.
distractors: Two is the dimensionless parameter and must be multiplied by √f(b).
Ten is the square root of certificate size before multiplying by t.
The stated scale gives 2·√100=20.
Two hundred multiplies by f(b), rather than by its square root.
teaching.takeaway: Certificate size controls a deficit scale; the product bound still includes a high-value event probability.
teaching.followup: If Pr(X≥100)≥1/2, what one-sided lower-tail bound follows at eighty?

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: After obtaining a Talagrand certificate bound around a median, a proof substitutes the mean without any further step. What is missing?
options: A bound comparing the median with the mean.
A proof that all graph functions are linear.
A claim that every random variable has equal mean and median.
Nothing: median and mean are interchangeable by definition.
questions.skill: Distinguish centers of concentration
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: A median controls at least half the probability on either side; a mean is an average. They need not coincide. Translating a median-centered tail to the mean requires a quantitative comparison, often derived by integrating a suitable tail estimate.
steps: Use the median to lower-bound the high-value event probability in the product inequality.
Derive the resulting one-sided tail with that specific center.
Only after bounding the mean–median separation may the threshold be rewritten around the mean, with the appropriate shift.
distractors: A quantitative center comparison is the required extra argument.
No universal linearity statement is relevant to the center change.
A skewed finite distribution already gives different mean and median.
Their definitions are different and do not imply numerical equality.
teaching.takeaway: Changing the center of a concentration inequality changes the statement.
teaching.followup: Construct a simple two- or three-point distribution with unequal mean and median.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: Let X count triangles in G(6,1/2). For the derivative-expectation convention E′=max over nonempty derivatives and E=max(E[X],E′), what are E′ and E?
questions.skill: Include every derivative order
questions.readingLabel: Worked example: triangle polynomial derivatives

teaching.summary: A triangle count is a degree-three polynomial in edge indicators. Its derivative scales include a full-triangle derivative equal to one; omitting that order gives an incorrect parameter even if some lower derivatives look smaller.
steps: A first-edge derivative has expectation 4(1/2)²=1; adjacent-edge second derivatives have expectation 1/2.
A derivative in all three edges of a triangle is one, so E′=1 and E=5/2.
distractors: These maxima include the third derivative and the larger zeroth-order mean correctly.
The nonempty-derivative maximum does not include the zeroth-order mean.
This omits both the first and third derivative values equal to one.
The triangle polynomial has nonzero derivatives, so E′ cannot vanish.
teaching.takeaway: Maximize over the entire derivative hierarchy named in the theorem.
teaching.followup: Repeat the calculation for general n and p and locate the sparse regime where a derivative dominates.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: For triangle count in G(n,p), the derivative with respect to two disjoint edge indicators is what?
questions.skill: Use the support of a polynomial derivative
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: Each triangle monomial contains three edges sharing three vertices. Two disjoint edges cannot both belong to one triangle, so differentiating by both removes every monomial from consideration.
steps: A monomial survives a mixed derivative only if it contains every differentiated variable.
Two disjoint edges have four endpoints and therefore cannot be contained in a triangle.
No monomial survives, giving the zero polynomial and derivative expectation zero.
distractors: A closing-edge indicator arises for two adjacent edges, not two disjoint edges.
One arises when differentiating all three edges of one triangle.
The support condition eliminates every triangle monomial.
A nontrivial derivative changes the polynomial and cannot leave the whole count intact.
teaching.takeaway: Derivative expectations reflect overlap structure, not just derivative order.
teaching.followup: Contrast adjacent-edge, disjoint-edge, and full-triangle derivatives.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: In the stated degree-k Kim–Vu failure bound dₖe⁻λN^{k−1}, triangle count in G(n,p) uses which N?
options: n, the number of graph vertices
C(n,3), the number of candidate triangles
C(n,2), the number of independent edge variables
questions.skill: Identify the theorem’s underlying independent coordinates
questions.readingLabel: Definitions & theorem: independent-variable and degree parameters

teaching.summary: Triangle indicators overlap and are dependent, whereas edge indicators form the independent input family. The N in this theorem counts those coordinates. The fixed degree is a separate parameter k=3.
steps: Write X as a polynomial in one Bernoulli variable xₑ for every potential edge.
There are C(n,2) independent inputs, so this is N.
The exponent N^{k−1} and constants must use the theorem’s convention; replacing N by n changes the advertised bound.
distractors: The graph vertex count is not the number of Bernoulli variables of this polynomial.
Candidate triangles are the dependent monomials, not the independent inputs.
Three is k, a distinct parameter from N.
Each potential edge supplies one independent Bernoulli coordinate.
teaching.takeaway: Before substituting a theorem, map every symbol to the modeled random object.
teaching.followup: Why is it invalid to apply an independent-summand Chernoff bound directly to the triangle indicators?

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: Encode a bit by 000 or 111 and decode by majority on a binary symmetric channel with crossover p=0.2. What is the error probability?
questions.skill: Compute a finite channel error exactly
questions.readingLabel: Worked example: repetition-code reliability

teaching.summary: Majority decoding fails when at least two of the three bits flip. The two-flip and three-flip events are disjoint, and their binomial probabilities must both be included.
steps: Exactly two flips occur with probability C(3,2)(0.2)²(0.8)=0.096.
Exactly three flips occur with probability (0.2)³=0.008.
Add the disjoint failure events to obtain 0.096+0.008=0.104.
distractors: This counts only the three-flip event and omits the dominant two-flip event.
This counts exactly two flips and omits three flips.
Both disjoint ways for the majority to be wrong are included.
This is one bit’s crossover probability, not the repetition decoder’s failure probability.
teaching.takeaway: A channel-error probability averages over allowed noise; it is not an all-pattern guarantee.
teaching.followup: Explain why this code corrects every single-bit error despite having positive channel error.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: For n=100, a decoding ball has at most 2^60 points. There are at most 2^30 competing words, independently uniform in {0,1}^100 and independent of the received word. Which expression is obtained by dividing ball volume by cube size and multiplying by the competitor count?
questions.skill: Derive the coding exponent from volume and rate
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: A fixed received word determines a ball. Each independently uniform competitor lands inside with probability at most the volume divided by the full cube size. The union bound then multiplies by the number of competitors.
steps: The ambient cube has 2^100 points, giving one-competitor probability at most 2^60/2^100=2^−40.
Union-bound at most 2^30 competing words: 2^30·2^−40=2^−10.
A complete reliability proof must additionally control the probability of atypical channel noise leaving this radius.
distractors: Subtracting ambient dimension from the two positive exponents gives negative ten.
This omits the decoding-ball volume or uses the wrong subtraction.
This is not the ratio of the ball volume to the ambient cube.
This multiplies counts without dividing by the ambient cube size.
teaching.takeaway: The entropy threshold compares codebook size times decoding volume with the whole cube.
teaching.followup: Which extra term must be added before concluding a bound on total decoding error?

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: A fixed codebook has average message error at most ε. What follows by discarding at most half its messages with the largest errors?
options: A linear code with efficient decoding.
A subcode with maximal error at most 2ε and rate loss at most 1/n.
Perfect correction of all corruption patterns.
Every original message already has error at most ε.
questions.skill: Separate average and maximal error
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: Markov’s inequality on the finite list of message errors gives a large set of individually good messages. Removing competing words cannot worsen their decoding error; no linear structure or efficient algorithm is created by this argument.
steps: At most half the messages can have individual error greater than 2ε, or their average alone would exceed ε.
Keep at least M/2 messages and restrict decoding to this subcode.
Its rate is at least (log₂M−1)/n, losing at most one bit per block, or 1/n in rate.
distractors: Expurgation does not prove linearity or efficient encoding and decoding.
The message-error averaging and the remaining codebook size give exactly this conclusion.
A small distributional error allows failures on rare corruption patterns.
An average bound permits some messages to be substantially worse.
teaching.takeaway: When the performance convention changes, supply the averaging or expurgation step explicitly.
teaching.followup: Why does expurgation generally destroy a linear-subspace structure?

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: Five candidates each permit one lie and four questions remain. With B(q,k)=2⁻ᑫΣⱼ≤ₖ C(q,j), what does the initial weight prove?
options: The weight is 5/16, so Paul wins.
The weight is 1, so the game is tied.
The weight is 25/16, so Carole can prevent unique identification.
The weight is 25, so there must be 25 candidates.
questions.skill: Use the Liar Game potential
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: Each candidate contributes the normalized size of its one-lie transcript allowance. A weight above one lets the adversary maintain an overloaded successor until the final state has at least two possible candidates.
steps: A candidate with four questions and one lie contributes (C(4,0)+C(4,1))/16=5/16.
Five such candidates give total weight 25/16>1.
The average-of-successors identity lets Carole choose a branch that does not decrease this potential.
distractors: Five-sixteenths is one candidate’s contribution, not the whole state’s weight.
The computed weight is strictly greater than one.
The potential exceeds one and supplies the adversary’s sufficient winning condition.
The weight is normalized by the sixteen possible answer strings.
teaching.takeaway: An overloaded normalized transcript budget can prove impossibility of unique identification.
teaching.followup: Explain why the final weight above one forces at least two surviving candidates.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: A legal question has successor weights 0.9 and 1.5. Which weight is their current parent weight, and which branch supports Carole’s invariant?
questions.skill: Read the average-of-successors identity
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: The normalized Liar Game weight is the average of the two legal successor weights. The adversary chooses the larger successor, so a parent state above one cannot be forced below one by the questioner.
steps: Use W=(WYes+WNo)/2, not their sum.
Carole selects the weight-1.5 branch, which preserves and increases the overloaded potential.
distractors: The parent is the average, and choosing the smaller successor can lose the invariant.
These are respectively the arithmetic average and the maximizing legal successor.
The average is not itself a legal successor unless the question produces that state.
The factor is one-half of the sum, not one-quarter.
teaching.takeaway: A potential argument must pair its identity with a legal branch-selection rule.
teaching.followup: Derive the same average identity from Pascal’s identity for B(q,k).

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: A Liar Game state has weight at most one. Why does that fact alone not exhibit a winning questioning strategy?
options: Low weight proves the adversary wins.
The state has no remaining candidates.
Weights are irrelevant in adaptive games.
A legal question must also split candidates so both successor states remain manageable.
questions.skill: Distinguish a capacity obstruction from a strategy
questions.readingLabel: Limits & counterexamples: weight versus adaptive strategy

teaching.summary: The weight calculation controls total capacity, but questions act on indivisible candidate states. A small total does not itself identify a legal partition that balances both possible responses throughout an adaptive tree.
steps: Weight above one gives an adversary strategy by selecting a high-weight successor.
The converse needs a questioner strategy, including the legal candidate split at every state.
Verify the two successor states and a terminal identification condition rather than treating a counting inequality as an algorithm.
distractors: The above-one condition, not its converse, supplies this adversary argument.
Positive candidate states can have arbitrarily small normalized weight.
Weights are useful, but do not automatically construct the missing split.
This is the additional constructive obligation absent from the weight inequality alone.
teaching.takeaway: A necessary counting condition is not automatically a sufficient adaptive strategy.
teaching.followup: State the quantifiers in “there exists a question whose every answer permits continuation.”

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: A Tenure position has one chip at level 1 and three chips at level 3. What is its dyadic weight and the threshold conclusion?
questions.skill: Apply the exact dyadic threshold
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: Positive levels contribute powers of two with negative exponents. The resulting total is below one, so the adversary can keep the weight below the value required by a level-zero chip.
steps: The near chip contributes 2^−1=1/2.
The three level-three chips contribute 3·2^−3=3/8, giving W=7/8.
Carole selects a successor no larger than the current weight, keeping W<1 and excluding level zero.
distractors: The computed weight is below the exact winning threshold for Paul.
This adds the level-three contributions incorrectly.
This treats the three distant chips as much heavier than their dyadic weights.
A weight below one is the adversary-winning side of this game’s exact threshold.
teaching.takeaway: Dyadic weight measures distance to tenure, not merely the number of chips.
teaching.followup: Which single additional positive-level chip would bring this state to weight at least one?

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: A state of total weight 1 is split into groups of weights 3/4 and 1/4. Surviving chips are promoted, doubling their weight. Why is this a poor split for Paul?
options: Both successors have weight at least one.
Carole can choose the smaller group, leaving weight 1/2.
The two successors have weights 3/4 and 1/4.
questions.skill: Make the potential invariant constructive
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: Paul’s threshold strategy needs a split with each group at least one-half before promotion. Merely starting with total weight one does not make every partition safe against the adversary.
steps: Promoting the first group gives weight 2·(3/4)=3/2.
Promoting the second group gives weight 2·(1/4)=1/2.
Carole chooses the latter; the resulting below-one state is on her winning side of the threshold.
distractors: Each surviving level decreases by one, doubling its dyadic contribution.
Only the larger successor stays above the threshold.
The adversary has a legal branch that breaks the intended invariant.
These are the pre-promotion group weights, not the successor-state weights.
teaching.takeaway: A winning potential needs a split that works against both responses.
teaching.followup: Find a safe split for one level-one chip together with two level-two chips.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: Why can two chips at level i be glued into one chip at level i−1 in the dyadic splitting lemma?
options: Their combined weight is unchanged and the number of chips decreases.
Their total weight doubles before any move.
The new chip always reaches level zero.
The move changes the legal threshold from one to two.
questions.skill: Understand the induction behind dyadic splitting
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: Gluing is a proof device for finding a balanced partition, not an extra move in the game. Equal dyadic pieces combine into the next larger dyadic piece, allowing induction on the number of chips.
steps: Two level-i weights sum to 2·2^−i=2^{−(i−1)}.
The total potential is preserved while the number of pieces falls by one.
After finding a partition of the glued pieces, replace the glued piece by its original pair on the same side.
distractors: The weight identity and smaller piece count justify the induction and its reversal.
The weight is preserved; actual promotion during the game is a different operation.
Only gluing level-one chips creates a level-zero piece in the proof representation.
The threshold remains one throughout the argument.
teaching.takeaway: An induction may simplify a representation without introducing a new legal game operation.
teaching.followup: Explain why ungluing preserves both group weights in the reconstructed partition.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: In six rounds, each coordinate is a simple symmetric walk under fresh fair Chooser signs, even against adaptive Pusher play. For one coordinate, what is Pr(|S₆|>4)?
questions.skill: Calculate an exact coordinate tail
questions.readingLabel: Worked example: a coordinate walk under adaptive play

teaching.summary: The only totals whose magnitude exceeds four are six and negative six. Each requires all six conditional coordinate increments to have the same sign; the fresh fair signs give the symmetric-walk law for this one coordinate.
steps: The possible totals are −6, −4, −2, 0, 2, 4, and 6.
Only the all-positive and all-negative increment strings give the two strict-tail outcomes.
Each has probability 2^−6, so the total is 2/64=1/32.
distractors: This counts only one of the two extreme directions.
The two extreme six-step paths are disjoint and equally likely.
This includes outcomes of magnitude four, which the strict inequality excludes.
The extreme walk outcomes are much rarer than this.
teaching.takeaway: Track strict versus non-strict thresholds when turning a walk into a tail event.
teaching.followup: Union-bound six such coordinate events without assuming the coordinates are independent.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: Why does an adaptive Pusher not change the fair conditional sign of one coordinate increment?
options: The current coordinate is fixed by the past, then multiplied by a fresh independent fair Chooser sign.
Pusher must choose the same vector at every round.
questions.skill: Condition on the correct game history
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: Pusher may exploit the entire past, but cannot anticipate the new independent random sign. Conditioning on the history fixes its current ±1 coordinate, so multiplying by a fair sign still yields a fair ±1 increment.
steps: Condition on all completed rounds and on the current vector selected by Pusher.
The fresh Chooser sign remains independent and takes each sign with probability one-half.
Multiplication by the now-fixed coordinate either preserves or swaps these two equally likely outcomes.
distractors: Pusher is explicitly allowed to adapt to previous rounds.
A common Chooser sign can strongly correlate different coordinates.
This conditional argument preserves fairness in each coordinate despite adaptation.
The vector may change arbitrarily with the legal game history.
teaching.takeaway: Adaptation to the past does not predict fresh independent randomness.
teaching.followup: Explain why the coordinate-wise walk law does not imply independence between coordinates.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: For every fixed Pusher strategy, random Chooser succeeds with positive probability. What does finite perfect-information game determinacy then imply?
options: One random seed works against every Pusher strategy.
The union bound proves the matching lower bound.
Both players can force success simultaneously.
Pusher has no forced win, so Chooser has a deterministic winning strategy for that target.
questions.skill: Respect the probability-to-strategy quantifiers
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: determinacy and randomized play

teaching.summary: Positive success against every fixed adversary rules out an adversary strategy that defeats every response. Determinacy supplies the complementary winning strategy, but does not identify a single random seed that succeeds against all adversaries.
steps: Assume Pusher had a strategy forcing Chooser to fail against every legal sequence of signs.
That same strategy would make random Chooser fail with probability one, contradicting the hypothesis.
By finite perfect-information determinacy, absence of a Pusher winning strategy gives a Chooser winning strategy.
distractors: This exchanges “for every strategy, some successful randomness” with a stronger uniform-seed claim.
An upper-bound argument does not automatically give a matching adversarial lower bound.
The opposing win conditions cannot both be forced in the same determined game.
This conclusion uses exactly the contradiction and determinacy steps.
teaching.takeaway: Do not exchange the order of strategy and randomness quantifiers.
teaching.followup: State what extra work would be needed to compute an efficient Chooser strategy.

questions.question: For fixed queries an item has truthful response string NNYNY. If at most one No may be changed to Yes, how many possible reported strings does it have?
questions.skill: Count one-sided error transcripts
questions.readingLabel: Worked example: one-sided response sets

teaching.summary: Only the three No positions can be altered. Each permitted one-lie choice gives a different reported string, and the truthful string is also allowed. Truthful Yes positions are not legal lie locations.
steps: The five-symbol truthful string has No at positions one, two, and four.
There are three distinct permitted single-lie reports and one no-lie report.
The total is four; a symmetric radius-one Hamming ball would incorrectly include two forbidden flips.
distractors: This counts the allowed single-lie choices but omits the truthful report.
Three eligible positions plus the no-lie string give four.
Five is the total question count and not the report-set size.
Six is the symmetric radius-one count, which allows the forbidden Yes-to-No flips.
teaching.takeaway: An asymmetric error model changes the transcript ball.
teaching.followup: How does the count change for a truthful string containing z No responses?

questions.question: Why cannot an adaptive Half-Liar argument silently identify every item with one fixed truthful bit string and use ordinary Hamming balls?
options: Adaptive questions may change after a lie, so later truthful answers follow a different path.
A truthful Yes can always be flipped to No.
No questions can be asked adaptively.
All items have the same truthful transcript.
questions.skill: Distinguish a decision tree from a fixed code
questions.readingLabel: Limits & counterexamples: fixed codes versus adaptive trees

teaching.summary: A nonadaptive questionnaire determines one fixed response coordinate system. An adaptive strategy chooses later questions from earlier reported answers, so the first lie can send the interaction to a different branch with different future questions.
steps: Locate the first reported response that differs from the truthful path.
After that divergence, evaluate the actual questions selected by the strategy on the new branch.
A correct counting or disjointness proof must compare these tree paths, rather than assume future coordinates stay fixed.
distractors: The branch-dependent future questions are the missing feature of a fixed-string argument.
This reverses the specified one-sided lie convention.
The game permits adaptive questioning; its analysis must model it.
A useful questioning strategy must distinguish different items, not assign them identical paths.
teaching.takeaway: Adaptive transcripts are paths whose later coordinates depend on earlier reports.
teaching.followup: Explain how a first-divergence argument can still count one-lie paths.
