questions.question: The assigned chapter works out the k=1 Half-Liar strategy and states a fixed-k asymptotic. Which claim is justified by reproducing only that k=1 proof?
options: A complete proof for every k growing with q.
A complete proof for every fixed k without another argument.
The k=1 case; higher-k and uniform-in-k statements require their own proof.
No result, because k=1 is not a fixed value.
questions.skill: Match proof scope to parameter scope
questions.readingLabel: Definitions & theorem: fixed-k scope and the k=1 proof

teaching.summary: A proof specialized to one permitted lie may exploit a two-level state structure unavailable for larger budgets. Stating a general theorem and proving one case are different accomplishments, and a fixed-k asymptotic does not cover k varying with q.
steps: Identify every place the strategy uses the distinction between unused and already-used single-lie states.
Record the demonstrated result with k explicitly set to one.
For a larger or varying budget, supply the additional state accounting and the relevant asymptotic uniformity.
distractors: Allowing k to grow changes the regime beyond a fixed-k asymptotic.
A specialized proof does not establish all other fixed values automatically.
This keeps the result aligned with the actual argument and its parameter range.
One is a legitimate fixed parameter and its theorem is meaningful.
teaching.takeaway: Keep theorem scope, proved special cases, and asymptotic regimes separate.
teaching.followup: What new state levels appear as soon as a second lie is allowed?

questions.question: Let X be uniform on {000,011,101,110}. Each pair of coordinates is independent. What is H(X₃|X₁,X₂)?
questions.skill: Distinguish pairwise from mutual independence
questions.readingLabel: Worked example: dependence and the chain rule

teaching.summary: The third bit is determined by the first two: it is their parity. Pairwise independence does not imply that a coordinate remains unpredictable after all preceding coordinates are revealed.
steps: The four pairs (X₁,X₂) occur with equal probability one-quarter.
For each pair the displayed family contains exactly one possible X₃, namely X₁+X₂ modulo two.
Every conditional distribution is a point mass, so its entropy and their average conditional entropy are zero.
distractors: Knowing the first two bits determines the third with certainty.
This is the entropy of the third bit before both determining bits are known.
Two bits is the entropy of the full four-point family.
Three bits is the sum of marginal entropies, which overcounts dependence.
teaching.takeaway: Pairwise independence can leave a deterministic higher-order constraint.
teaching.followup: Use the chain rule to recover H(X)=2 although all three marginal entropies equal one.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: Choose X uniformly from F={00,01,10}. The first-coordinate projection has two values. Which statement is correct?
options: X₁ is uniform because X is uniform.
Every projection has the same distribution as X.
questions.skill: Use support bounds without assuming projection uniformity
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: Uniformity on the original family weights projected values by the sizes of their fibers. The first coordinate has two preimages at zero and one at one, so its entropy is strictly below the logarithm of its two-point support.
steps: List the fibers: first-coordinate zero comes from 00 and 01, while one comes only from 10.
Thus the first bit has probabilities 2/3 and 1/3, not equal probabilities.
The entropy maximum on two points is one bit, attained only by the fair distribution.
distractors: Uniform sampling does not make differently sized projection fibers equiprobable.
The full-vector entropy is log₂3, not the entropy of its first bit.
This distinguishes the exact marginal law from its valid support-size upper bound.
A projection has fewer coordinates and generally a different distribution.
teaching.takeaway: A projection need not be uniform; its entropy is nevertheless bounded by log support size.
teaching.followup: Compute H₂(1/3) and locate the strict inequality in an entropy projection proof.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: A uniform nonempty binary family F attains H(X)=ΣᵢH(Xᵢ). What structural condition follows?
options: Every coordinate must be a fair bit.
The coordinates are mutually independent, and F is a Cartesian product of its coordinate supports.
F can have any shape if its size is large enough.
questions.skill: Read the equality case
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: Equality in entropy subadditivity requires that the coordinates carry no dependence. For a uniform distribution supported on F, an independent joint law has support equal to the product of the marginal supports, forcing the same Cartesian structure on F.
steps: The chain-rule proof compares each conditional entropy with its marginal entropy.
Equality of their sum forces equality at every nonnegative information-loss term, yielding mutual independence.
Independence gives product support; binary coordinate supports may be a singleton or both values.
distractors: Fixed coordinates are allowed and have zero entropy; not every coordinate must be fair.
Mutual independence and product support are the equality-case consequences.
A parity family is pairwise independent but has strict entropy subadditivity.
Entropy equality imposes dependence constraints regardless of family size.
teaching.takeaway: Equality cases often encode the structure discarded by a proof inequality.
teaching.followup: Why can no three-member binary family attain this equality?

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: For coordinates {1,2,3}, use projection sets {1,2} and {2,3}. What is the largest k satisfying Shearer’s uniform coverage condition?
questions.skill: Count the minimum coordinate multiplicity
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: The coverage requirement applies to every coordinate, not the average. Although coordinate two appears twice, coordinates one and three appear only once, so the common multiplicity cannot exceed one.
steps: Count appearances: coordinate one occurs in the first set only, coordinate two in both, and coordinate three in the second only.
The three multiplicities are 1, 2, and 1.
Their minimum is one, giving H(X)≤H(X₁,X₂)+H(X₂,X₃), without a factor two on the left.
distractors: Every coordinate is covered at least once, so zero is not the largest valid k.
The least-covered coordinates each occur once.
This uses the central coordinate’s multiplicity and ignores both endpoints.
No coordinate occurs in three sets when there are only two sets.
teaching.takeaway: Shearer’s multiplicity is a minimum over coordinates, not a total or average.
teaching.followup: Construct a product family showing why replacing k=1 by k=2 is false.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: A finite three-coordinate family has pairwise projection sizes at most 4, 6, and 6. What is the smallest listed cardinality upper bound yielded by the Loomis–Whitney projection calculation?
questions.skill: Convert an entropy inequality to an integer count
questions.readingLabel: Worked example: the three projection factors

teaching.summary: The three pairwise projections cover every coordinate twice. Shearer therefore bounds the square of the full-family size by the product of the three support sizes; taking the square root is the final step.
steps: Each coordinate lies in exactly two of the xy, xz, and yz projection sets.
The cardinality inequality gives |F|²≤4·6·6=144.
Because |F| is nonnegative, take square roots to get |F|≤12.
distractors: Sixteen is not the square root of the stated projection product.
This is the upper bound on |F|² before taking the root.
This does not use the required cover multiplicity two correctly.
The product is 144 and the common multiplicity is two.
teaching.takeaway: Convert the projection-cover multiplicity into the correct root of the product.
teaching.followup: Find a Cartesian box with these exact three projection sizes.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: In the chain-rule proof, why is H(Xᵢ | earlier coordinates lying in S) ≥ H(Xᵢ | all earlier coordinates)?
options: The left conditions on less information, so its uncertainty can be larger.
The two sides are equal for every distribution.
questions.skill: Keep the conditioning inequality in the correct direction
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: Adding conditioning variables cannot increase conditional entropy. A projection forgets some earlier coordinates, so its chain-rule term is at least the corresponding full-history term. Summing these lower bounds produces Shearer’s inequality.
steps: The earlier coordinates of S form a subset of the complete earlier-coordinate set.
Conditioning on the remaining earlier coordinates can reveal additional information about Xᵢ.
Therefore the projected conditional entropy is the larger side; coverage counts copies of the smaller full-history term.
distractors: This correctly compares the two conditioning sets and the resulting uncertainty.
The general monotonicity is the opposite direction when adding conditioning.
Uniformity of projections is unnecessary and often false.
Dependence can make the inequality strict, as a repeated-bit example shows.
teaching.takeaway: Determine which conditioning set is larger before choosing an entropy-inequality direction.
teaching.followup: Use X₂=X₁ to show a strict instance of this conditioning comparison.

questions.question: In a sampled three-leaf star, one branch colors the independent leaves red, blue, green, leaving the center with no available color. May a one-sided 3-colorability tester reject on this basis alone?
options: Yes, an empty list on any branch proves non-3-colorability.
No: this branch fails, but the star is two-colorable and another branch succeeds.
No graph can have an empty color list.
questions.skill: Distinguish one failed coloring from an obstruction
questions.readingLabel: Limits & counterexamples: all branches of a restriction tree

teaching.summary: A one-sided tester must never reject a graph that has the property. The displayed branch chooses incompatible leaf colors unnecessarily; assigning every leaf the same color and the center another color gives a valid coloring.
steps: The star’s leaves have no edges between them, so they may all share one color.
Color the center with a second color to obtain a proper two-coloring.
Failure of one partial assignment is not failure of every branch of the restriction tree.
distractors: An empty list certifies failure only of that partial coloring.
A star has no triangle, let alone a four-clique.
An explicit proper coloring disproves the proposed rejection certificate.
Empty lists can occur after poor partial choices, as the example shows.
teaching.takeaway: One-sided rejection requires a genuine obstruction, not a failed greedy attempt.
teaching.followup: Why does the K₄ example fail under every proper choice for its first three vertices?

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: A restriction-tree branch starts with total feasible-list size at most 3n. Each restricting step removes at least εn entries, giving depth d≤3/ε. For ε=1/8, what is the numerical value of this n-independent bound 3/ε?
questions.skill: Translate potential decrease into branch depth
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: The initial potential and the per-step decrease both contain n, so their ratio is independent of graph size. This is one reason a bounded sampling argument can be built from the restriction tree.
steps: The nonnegative list-size potential begins at at most 3n.
After d restricting steps it has fallen by at least dεn, hence dεn≤3n.
Cancel n and substitute ε=1/8 to obtain d≤3/ε=24.
distractors: Eight is 1/ε and omits the three initial color choices per vertex.
The ratio of the total potential to the minimum decrement is twenty-four.
This is the starting potential, not a depth after dividing by the decrement.
This confuses the decrement’s scale with the number of possible decrements.
teaching.takeaway: A nonnegative potential bounds the number of large-decrease steps by initial value divided by decrement.
teaching.followup: Explain why bounding a single branch is still not enough to establish the full tester’s soundness.

questions.question: The dense-graph model normalizes edit distance by n². For n=1000, what edit count equals εn² when ε=0.01?
questions.skill: Use the stated distance convention
questions.readingLabel: Definitions & theorem: dense-graph edit distance

teaching.summary: The chapter’s normalization is by n squared, not by the number of unordered pairs. Keeping the convention explicit prevents a factor-two mismatch when moving between theorem statements or testing models.
steps: Square the vertex count to obtain n²=1,000,000.
Multiply by ε=0.01 to obtain 10,000 edits.
This is the benchmark in the stated model; using C(n,2) instead would define a different numerical normalization.
distractors: This multiplies the fraction by n instead of by n squared.
One thousand omits the additional factor from squaring n.
This roughly uses the unordered-pair count instead of the specified n² normalization.
One percent of one million is ten thousand.
teaching.takeaway: Distance parameters are meaningful only with their normalization and allowed edit operations.
teaching.followup: Explain what “ε-far from 3-colorable” asserts about every proper-coloring repair.

questions.question: A fixed graph on eight vertices contains seven triangles. What is the probability that one uniform unordered vertex-triple sample finds a triangle?
questions.skill: Use the exact finite sample space
questions.readingLabel: Worked example: triple sampling

teaching.summary: A uniform unordered triple ranges over C(8,3) equally likely choices, not all ordered triples with repetition. The graph determines which of these choices are favorable.
steps: There are C(8,3)=56 unordered triples of distinct vertices.
Exactly seven of those triples induce a triangle by the given count.
The hit probability is 7/56=1/8.
distractors: Seven favorable triples among fifty-six gives one-eighth.
Sixty-four is not the number of unordered triples on eight vertices.
The number of triangles is not the denominator of the sampling space.
This divides by the vertex count instead of the triple count.
teaching.takeaway: Use the sampling distribution’s actual denominator before taking asymptotic approximations.
teaching.followup: For q independent triple samples, write the exact miss probability.

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: Each independent triple sample detects a triangle with probability 1/8. Which is the exact probability that all ten samples miss?
questions.skill: Multiply independent misses
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: The graph is fixed and the trials are independent selections with replacement. A trial misses with probability seven-eighths; all ten missing is their intersection, so their probabilities multiply.
steps: Complement the single-trial hit probability to obtain a miss probability 7/8.
Independence of the repeated samples gives ten identical factors.
The exact miss probability is (7/8)^10, while exp(−10/8) is a useful upper bound, not an equality.
distractors: A union-bound subtraction can be negative and is not an exact independent-trial calculation.
This is the probability that every trial hits a triangle.
The ten independent miss events each contribute a factor seven-eighths.
Independence multiplies probabilities; it does not divide by the number of trials.
teaching.takeaway: A sampling proof distinguishes an exact product from its exponential upper bound.
teaching.followup: Derive q≥8 ln(1/η) as a sufficient sample count for miss probability at most η.

questions.question: The triangle-removal lemma supplies a positive δ(ε). Why can the resulting tester be constant-query in n yet impractical?
options: The graph must have finitely many vertices.
δ(ε) can be extremely small, making the required number of samples huge.
Constant-query means exactly one edge query.
The lemma promises an efficient dependence on ε automatically.
questions.skill: Separate graph-size independence from parameter efficiency
questions.readingLabel: Definitions & theorem: the removal function

teaching.summary: For each fixed distance threshold ε the structural lemma yields a positive abundance bound, allowing a sample count independent of n. The value of that bound may deteriorate severely as ε decreases, and its reciprocal drives the sampling cost.
steps: Farness implies at least δ(ε)n³ triangles, giving a positive detection probability determined by ε.
Choose enough independent triples to make the miss probability small; the count scales with the reciprocal abundance.
Independence from n does not place a practical upper bound on this ε-dependent constant.
distractors: Finiteness is not the source of a poor distance-parameter dependence.
A tiny removal function makes a valid asymptotic tester expensive.
Constant-query means a bound independent of n for fixed ε, not one query.
Quantitative efficiency requires additional bounds on the removal function.
teaching.takeaway: State which parameter a “constant” is allowed to depend on.
teaching.followup: Identify exactly where the removal lemma enters the probability calculation.

questions.question: The induced subgraph on four vertices has the cycle edges of C₄ and one diagonal. Does it contain an ordinary C₄ and an induced C₄ on these vertices?
options: Ordinary C₄ yes; induced C₄ no
questions.skill: Check nonedges in an induced pattern
questions.readingLabel: Worked example: ordinary versus induced four-cycles

teaching.summary: An ordinary copy needs only the required cycle edges. An induced copy also forbids both diagonals. Adding a diagonal leaves the cycle as a subgraph but changes the full induced adjacency pattern.
steps: The four cycle edges are present, so they still form an ordinary C₄.
An induced C₄ requires each of the two diagonal pairs to be absent.
The added diagonal violates that nonedge requirement on the four sampled vertices.
distractors: The required four cycle edges still give an ordinary copy.
The extra diagonal prevents the induced copy despite preserving the ordinary one.
An induced copy would also be an ordinary copy, and here inducedness fails.
This distinguishes required edges from the additional forbidden edges.
teaching.takeaway: Induced testing checks the entire sampled adjacency pattern, including nonedges.
teaching.followup: Why is induced-C₄-freeness hereditary but not necessarily preserved by edge deletion?

questions.subject: probability

questions.question: Which property is hereditary under taking induced subgraphs but is not closed under arbitrary edge deletion?
questions.skill: Separate vertex-hereditary from edge-monotone properties
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board

teaching.summary: An induced subgraph of an induced-C₄-free graph cannot acquire a new induced C₄, because its relevant adjacencies are unchanged. Edge deletion is different: removing the two diagonals of K₄ creates an induced C₄.
steps: K₄ contains no induced C₄ because every four-vertex induced graph is complete.
Delete two opposite edges to leave a four-cycle with both diagonals absent.
Thus induced-C₄-freeness survives induced vertex restrictions but can fail after edge deletion.
distractors: The K₄-to-C₄ deletion example shows exactly this distinction.
Deleting edges cannot create a triangle, so triangle-freeness is edge-deletion closed.
Deleting edges preserves every proper two-coloring of a bipartite graph.
Deleting edges preserves the property of already having none.
teaching.takeaway: Hereditary and edge-deletion-monotone are different closure conditions.
teaching.followup: Explain why adding edges can destroy an induced forbidden pattern.

questions.question: A hereditary property has an infinite family of forbidden induced graphs. What supplies a finite sample bound for its one-sided tester at a fixed ε?
options: Assume the forbidden family is secretly finite.
Use ordinary triangle removal for every property.
Use the induced-removal/testability input giving an ε-dependent witness-size and abundance bound.
Test only the smallest forbidden graph, regardless of ε.
questions.skill: Identify the structural theorem needed by the tester
questions.readingLabel: Proof at the board: induced-removal as a stated input

teaching.summary: The forbidden-family characterization alone may involve graphs of unbounded size. The deep structural input says that ε-farness forces a detectable bounded-size induced obstruction, with bounds depending on the property and ε. That implication makes finite sampling possible.
steps: Hereditary closure characterizes membership by avoiding the full forbidden induced family.
The testability/removal theorem turns farness into bounded-size witness abundance at the chosen ε.
Sample enough vertices to expose such a witness; a graph with the property cannot be falsely rejected by it.
distractors: An infinite forbidden family need not reduce to a finite one globally.
Ordinary triangle removal does not enforce arbitrary induced edge-and-nonedge patterns.
This is the additional quantitative structural input used to construct the tester.
The smallest obstruction alone may miss graphs far from the property.
teaching.takeaway: A characterization of membership is not yet a quantitative sampling theorem.
teaching.followup: Which parts of the one-sided tester are elementary once the induced-removal input is granted?
